The Parable of a Woman Seeking Another Son; (1) The Parable of the Fool Eating Salt. **The Parable of the Fool Eating Salt (I)** Once there was a fool who went to another's house. When the host served him food, he complained that it was bland and lacked flavor. Upon hearing this, the host added more salt.
Having obtained salt and found it delicious, he thought to himself:
"The reason it is so delicious is because of the salt; if even a small amount is like this, how much more so would a large amount be?
The foolish man, lacking wisdom, then began to eat salt on its own. Having finished eating, his mouth became acrid, and it instead became a source of affliction for him.

It is like those non-Buddhists who, hearing that one may attain the Way by restricting one's food and drink, immediately cease eating for seven days or even fifteen days; they merely exhaust themselves with hunger, which is of no benefit to the Way.
Just as that foolish man, because he desired the flavor of salt, ate it alone and caused his mouth to become bitter, so too is this case. 2.

The Parable of the Fool Gathering Milk (II): The Parable of the Fool Gathering Milk Long ago, there was a fool who intended to entertain guests and wished to collect milk to provide for them. He thought to himself:
"If I were to milk the cows in advance every day, the milk would gradually accumulate until there is no place to store it, or else it will turn sour."
"It would be better to place it inside the cow's belly and wait until the time of the assembly to milk it all at once.
Having had this thought, he then seized both the mother cow and her calf and tied them separately in different places.
One month later, he prepared a feast and invited his guests; he then brought the cow forward, intending to milk it, but its milk had already dried up and was gone.
At that time, among the assembled guests, some may become angry and others laugh.
It is the same with the fool who wishes to practice giving; he says, "I shall wait until I am very wealthy, and only then will I give all at once."

Before they have even gathered, they may be seized by officials, fire, water, or thieves; or they may suddenly pass away before they can be given as a timely gift—of such a nature is that [merit] as well.

3. The Parable of the Fool Struck on the Head with a Pear (III) Once there was a fool whose head was hairless. At that time, another person struck his head with a pear; this happened a second and even a third time, yet his head was wounded and split open each time. Throughout it all, the fool remained silent and endured it, not knowing how to move away.
A bystander, having seen this, said to him:
"Why did you not move away, but instead remain there to receive these blows until your head was broken?
The fool replied:

"That man was arrogant and relied on his strength; being foolish and lacking wisdom, he saw that there were no hairs upon my head and took me for a stone, so he struck my head with a pear until it was thus shattered."
A bystander said to him:
"You yourself are foolish; why do you call him 'foolish'?
If you were not foolish, would you have been beaten by him until your head was split open without knowing how to escape?"

The bhikṣu is likewise: unable to fully cultivate faith, precepts, learning, and wisdom, he merely arranges his deportment to attract gain and offerings. He is like that foolish man who, when struck on the head by another, does not know to avoid it; even until he is wounded and broken, he instead accuses the other of being foolish. This bhikṣu is just the same.
4. The Parable of the Wife Who Feigned Death (IV) The Parable of the Wife Who Feigned Death: Long ago, there was a foolish man whose wife was beautiful and whom he cherished deeply.

However, the wife lacked integrity and faith; subsequently, she consorted with another man. Her illicit passion grew intense, and desiring to pursue her paramour and abandon her husband, she spoke secretly to an old woman, saying:
"After I have gone away, you should take the corpse of a dead woman and place it in our house, then tell my husband that I am already dead."
Later, when her husband was away, the old woman placed a corpse inside his house.
When her husband returned, the old woman said to him,
"Your wife has already died."

The husband immediately went to look and, seeing that it was indeed his wife, he wept and lamented in grief. He gathered a great quantity of firewood and oil to cremate her remains, and he placed the bones in a bag, carrying them with him day and night.
Later, the woman grew weary of her paramour and returned home, saying to her husband,
"I am your wife. Her husband replied to her:
"My wife died long ago; who are you to falsely claim she is my wife?
He spoke thus even a second and a third time, yet he still did not believe him.

Just as those non-Buddhists (tīrthika), upon hearing false doctrines from others, develop attachment through delusion and claim them to be the truth that can never be altered, they do not believe in, accept, or uphold the true teaching even when they hear it.

5. The Parable of Seeing Water in a Thirsty Man (V) In the past, there was a man who was deluded and lacked wisdom. Being extremely thirsty and in need of water, he saw a mirage in the heat of the sun and took it to be water. He immediately ran after it until he reached the Indus River; yet, once at the river’s edge, he gazed at it but did not drink.
A bystander said to him, "You were suffering from thirst and pursued water; now that you have reached the water's edge, why do you not drink?
The fool replied:
"You may drink it all up; I shall drink it as well. However, this water is so vast that neither of us could exhaust it; for this reason, we do not drink.
When the multitude heard these words, they all laughed loudly in derision.

For example, it is like the heterodox practitioners who perversely grasp at principles; because they are unable to fully uphold the Buddha’s precepts, they refuse to receive them altogether, thereby ensuring that in the future they will lack the capacity for attaining the Way and will continue to transmigrate through birth and death. This is just like those foolish people who see water but do not drink it, and are thus ridiculed by others. It is exactly the same in this case.
6. The Parable of the Foolish Man Who Wished to Keep His Dead Son at Home (Six) Once there was a foolish man who raised seven sons; one of them died first.
At that time, when this foolish man saw that his son was dead, he wished to leave him in the house while intending to depart himself.
Seeing this, a bystander said to him: "The paths of life and death are different;
you ought to quickly prepare [the body] and transport it to a distant place for burial. How can you keep him here and intend to abandon him yourself?"
At that time, having heard these words, the foolish man thought to himself:
"If I cannot delay it and must indeed bury him, I must kill another son to serve as a counterweight at the other end of the pole; only then will I be able to carry him."
Thereupon, he killed another of his sons and carried him away to bury him deep in the forest wilderness.
When people of the time saw this, they were deeply moved by derision and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.

For example, suppose a bhikṣu has privately violated a single precept; out of reluctance to reform and repent, he remains silent and conceals it, claiming for himself that he is pure. Should someone who knows of this say to him:

"One who has left the household life upholds the prohibitive precepts as one guards a bright pearl, ensuring they do not become marred. Why have you now violated what you received and yet desire not to confess?"
The precept-breaker said,
"If one must indeed perform repentance, let us commit further offenses first, and then we shall emerge. Thereupon,
he broke the precepts and committed many unwholesome acts, only then suddenly emerging.
Just as that fool, having already lost one son, went on to kill another, so too is this bhikṣu now. 7.

The Parable of Recognizing Someone as One’s Brother (VII) The Parable of Recognizing Someone as One’s Brother: Once there was a man of handsome appearance and full wisdom, who possessed great wealth; among all the people of the world, there were none who did not praise him.
At that time, there was a foolish man who, seeing this, said, "He is my elder brother.
The reason he spoke thus was that because the other possessed wealth which could be used whenever needed, he considered him his brother;
yet, seeing him repay his debts, he said, "He is not my brother."
A bystander said to him: "You are a fool!
Why do you require wealth and yet call another your elder brother?"
When it came time for him to pay the debt, he again claimed, "He is not my elder brother.

The foolish man replied, "I recognized him as my elder brother only because I desired his wealth; in truth, he is not my brother. If it were a matter of debt, then I would claim he is not my brother."
When people heard these words, there was none who did not laugh at them.

It is like those non-Buddhists who, upon hearing the Buddha’s excellent teachings, greedily plagiarized them and claimed them as their own; even when bystanders instructed them to practice, they refused to do so, saying:
"For the sake of profit and offerings, he has taken the Buddha's words to convert sentient beings, yet there is no reality to them—how could one possibly practice?"

"It is just as when one speaks to a fool for the sake of gaining wealth, saying, 'This is my elder brother,' yet when it comes time to pay a debt, one says again, 'He is not my brother. This case is exactly like that.

8. The Parable of the Mountain Qiang Who Stole from the State Treasury (Eight) The Parable of the Mountain Qiang Who Stole from the State Treasury: In a past age, there was a mountain Qiang who stole goods from the royal treasury and fled far away.
At that time, the king dispatched men in all directions to search for and capture him, bringing him before the king.
The king immediately questioned him regarding the source of the garments he had obtained.
The mountain tribesman replied, "These garments of mine were the property of my ancestors."

The King sent garments for them to wear, but as these were not originally possessed by the mountain tribesmen, they did not know how to put them on; what should have been worn on the hands was placed upon their feet, and what should have been worn at the waist was instead placed upon their heads.
Having seen the thieves, the king assembled his ministers to deliberate on the matter and said to them:
"If these are garments that have belonged to your ancestors since time immemorial, you ought to wear them properly; why have you inverted them, using the upper for the lower?"
Because he does not understand, it is certain that your robe must have been stolen; it is not your original possession. This is used as a metaphor:

the King is like the Buddha, the treasure store is like the Dharma, and the foolish Qiang man is like the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Having overheard the Buddha’s Dharma, they incorporate it into their own doctrines, claiming it as their own. Yet, because they do not understand, they arrange the Buddha’s Dharma in a way that confuses those above and below, failing to recognize the true characteristics of the Dharma.
It is just like that mountain tribesman who obtained the king’s precious robe; not knowing the proper order, he put it on in a reversed manner, and it was exactly like this. 9.
The Parable of Praising One’s Father’s Virtue (Nine) The Parable of Praising One’s Father’s Virtue: Long ago, there was a man who, in the midst of a great crowd, praised his father’s virtues, saying:
"My father is compassionate and benevolent; he does not harm others nor steal. He always speaks the truth and practices generosity as well."
At that time, there was a foolish man who, upon hearing these words, thought to himself:
"My father’s virtuous conduct surpasses even yours.
The people asked him:
"What virtuous conduct do you possess? Please explain the matter.
The fool replied, "Since my childhood, my father has severed all sexual desire and has never been stained by impurity."
The people said to him,
"If you have severed lustful desire, how could you be born?
He was deeply mocked and ridiculed by the people of the time.

It is just as when those in the world who lack wisdom, wishing to praise another's virtue but failing to recognize its reality, instead bring about censure; like that fool whose intention was to extol his father but whose words resulted in a fault, this case is exactly the same.

10. The Simile of the Three-Story Mansion (10) In times past, there was a wealthy man who was foolish and ignorant. While visiting the house of another wealthy man, he saw a three-story mansion that was high, vast, magnificent, spacious, and bright. His heart was filled with longing, and he thought to himself:
"My wealth is no less than his; why have I not built such a mansion during all this time?"
He immediately summoned a carpenter and asked him,
"Are you skilled at building that kind of elegant house?
The carpenter replied:
"This was my doing," he said, and then spoke these words:
"Now, you must build a tower for me just like that one."
At that time, the carpenter immediately measured the ground, stacked bricks, and built a multi-storied tower.
When the fool saw him stacking bricks to build the house, he remained full of doubt and could not understand it, so he asked him:
"What do you intend to make?"
The carpenter replied,
"I shall build a three-storied house.
The fool spoke again:
"I do not wish for a two-story house; first, you should build the upper story for me.
The carpenter replied, "That is impossible.
How can one construct a second story without first building the lowest story?"
"If the second story has not been built, how can the third story be constructed?
The fool insisted, saying, "I have no need for the lower two stories; you must build the topmost one for me."
When the people heard this, they were struck with wonder and laughter, all saying:
"How can one obtain the upper [level] without first constructing the lower and first house?

It is like the fourfold assembly of the World-Honored One’s disciples, who, unable to practice with diligence and reverence toward the Triple Gem, yet being indolent and lazy while desiring to seek the fruits of the Path, speak these words:
"I have no further need for the remaining three fruits; I seek only that fruit of arhatship.
He was thus ridiculed by the people of the time, being no different from those fools.

11. The Parable of the Brahmin Who Killed His Son (11). The Parable of the Brahmin Who Killed His Son: Long ago, there was a brahmin who considered himself highly learned; he was thoroughly proficient in all forms of astrology and various arts and crafts. Relying on such self-assurance and wishing to display his virtue, he traveled to another kingdom and went about weeping while cradling a child in his arms.
Someone asked the brahmin,
"Why are you weeping?
The brahmin replied:
"This child shall die in seven days; I weep for him only out of pity for such an untimely death.
The people of the time said, "The span of human life is difficult to know, and calculations are prone to error. Even if the seventh day arrives, he might not die; why do you weep in advance?"
The Brahmin said,
"The sun and moon may grow dark and the stars may fall, but what I have predicted shall never fail.
For the sake of fame and profit, on the seventh day, he killed his own son to prove his words.
At that time, when the people of the world heard seven days later that his son had died, they all sighed in admiration, saying, "Truly he was a wise man; what he said was not mistaken.
With hearts filled with faith and conviction, they all came to pay their respects.

It is just as when the fourfold assembly of the Buddha’s disciples, for the sake of gain and offerings, claimed to have attained the Way; such were the ways of foolish men who killed virtuous sons and falsely manifested the virtue of compassion, thereby causing them to suffer endlessly in the future—just as the Brahmin, to verify his own words, killed his son to delude the world.
12. The Parable of Boiling Black Molasses (12) The Parable of Boiling Black Molasses: Once upon a time, there was a foolish man boiling black molasses when a wealthy man came to his house.
At that time, this foolish man thought to himself:
"I shall now take some black honey-syrup and give it to this wealthy man.
He then added a small amount of water and placed it over the fire.
He then fanned the fire with a fan, hoping to make it cool.
A bystander said to him,
"If you do not stop the fire below, how can you expect to make it cool by fanning it incessantly?"
At that time, the entire multitude laughed in derision.

It is just like those heterodox practitioners who do not extinguish the blazing fire of their afflictions; though they perform slight asceticism—lying upon beds of thorns or scorching their bodies with the five heats—they hope for the path of coolness and tranquility. This can never come to pass; they merely become objects of wonder and laughter for the wise, suffering now while the calamities flow on into future kalpas.

13. The Parable of the Man Who Liked Anger (Thirteen) The Parable of the Man Who Liked Anger: In the past, there was a man who sat among a great multitude of people inside a house and praised the excellent virtues of a certain outsider, saying that he had only two faults:
first, he was prone to anger; second, he acted with haste.

At that time, this man was standing outside the gate; hearing these words, he immediately gave rise to anger, entered the house, seized that person who had called him foolish and wicked, and struck him with his hand.
A bystander asked,
"For what reason did you strike him?
The man replied:
"When have I ever delighted in anger or acted with haste?
Yet this person says:
'I delight in anger and act with haste.'"
"This is why I struck him.
A bystander said, "The signs of your current delight in anger and your impulsive nature have been immediately revealed; how can you deny them?"
When people speak of one's grave transgressions and give rise to resentment and reproach, the world deeply deems such a person foolish and deluded.

It is like a man in the world who drinks wine; addicted and immersed in liquor, he commits various acts of negligence. When others see him and rebuke him, he instead gives rise to resentment and anger, bitterly citing proofs and arguments to try to make himself clear. Just so, this fool avoids hearing of his own faults; when he sees others speaking of them, he instead wishes to strike and beat them.

14. The Parable of the Merchant Leader Killed for Sacrifice to Heaven (14) In the past, there was a merchant who wished to enter the great ocean. According to the essential rules for entering the great ocean, one must have a guide before proceeding; thus, they sought and found a guide. Having obtained him, they set out together and reached the midst of a vast wilderness.
There was a shrine that required human sacrifice before one could pass through;
thereupon, the merchants deliberated together, saying, "Our entire caravan consists of kinsmen and relatives—how can we kill them?"
"We shall use this leader alone as the sacrificial offering for Heaven.
They then killed the leader to perform the sacrifice.
Once the sacrifice to Heaven was completed, they lost their way and did not know where to go; they perished in poverty and exhaustion.
All people of the world are likewise thus: desiring to enter the sea of Dharma to obtain its precious treasures, they should cultivate the practice of wholesome dharmas to serve as their guide.

If they destroy their wholesome conduct, they will remain forever without a time of emergence upon the vast road of birth and death; they will pass through the three miserable realms and suffer for a long duration, just like those merchants who, about to enter the great ocean, kill their guide and lose the way to the crossing, ultimately meeting with exhaustion and death.

15. The Parable of the Physician Giving Medicine to the King’s Daughter So That She Grows Up Instantly (15) Once there was a king who gave birth to a daughter. He summoned a physician and said to him:
"Give me medicine so that she may grow up immediately."
The physician replied, "I have an excellent medicine that can cause it to grow large immediately; however, it is not currently available and must first be sought out.
During the interval until the medicine is obtained, Your Majesty must not look at it; wait until the medicine has been administered, and only then shall it be shown to you."

Thereupon, he traveled far to fetch the medicine; after twelve years, having obtained it, he returned and gave it to the girl to take. He then presented it to the king, who, seeing it, was filled with joy and thought to himself:
"Truly, this is a skilled physician; the medicine he has given my daughter is able to cause her to grow so suddenly."
He then commanded his attendants to bestow precious jewels upon him.

At that time, the people laughed at the king’s lack of wisdom, for he did not understand how to calculate the boy's age from his birth; seeing only that the boy had grown large, they believed it was due to the power of the medicine.
People of the world are likewise; they approach a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and address them, saying:
"I wish to seek the Way and pray that you will instruct me, so that I may attain it immediately.

Out of skillful means (*upāya*), the spiritual friend teacher instructs them to practice seated meditation (*dhyāna*) and contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). By gradually accumulating manifold virtues, they attain the state of an Arhat, whereupon they leap for joy with redoubled delight and speak these words:
"How wonderful, Great Master!
You have been able to cause me to realize the most sublime Dharma so swiftly!
16. The Parable of the Sugarcane (16) The Parable of the Sugarcane: In the past, there were two men who together planted sugarcane and made this vow:
"Those who plant well shall be rewarded; those who do not plant well shall be severely punished.
At that time, one among the two men thought to himself:
"Sugar cane is extremely sweet. If one were to press it to extract the juice and pour it back onto the sugar cane tree, its sweetness would surely become even greater, surpassing that of the others."
He immediately crushed the sugarcane to extract the juice for irrigation, hoping for a sweet flavor, yet instead he ruined the seeds and lost all the sugarcane.

People of the world are just like this: desiring to seek merit and blessings, they rely on their own wealth and nobility, using forceful intimidation and power to coerce the common people and seize their property. They take this as the basis for performing meritorious deeds, expecting good fruits in the future; unaware that in the end they will instead incur calamity and disaster, just like crushing sugarcane where both parties lose everything.

17. The Parable of the Half-Coin Debt (17). Regarding the parable of the half-coin debt: Long ago, there was a merchant who had lent another person half a coin but had not recovered it for a long time. He then went to demand repayment.

There was a great river ahead; he had to pay two coins to hire a ferryman before he could cross it. Upon reaching his destination, he went to collect the debt but could not find the man. When he returned to cross back over the river, he again had to pay two coins to hire a ferryman.

For the sake of a debt of half a coin, he lost four coins; moreover, he suffered from the exhaustion and fatigue of the journey. Thus, for a very small debt, he lost an immense amount, and was consequently ridiculed by the multitude.

People of the world are likewise; for the sake of a little fame and profit, they ruin their great conduct, seeking only to accommodate themselves while disregarding propriety and righteousness. Thus they incur an evil reputation in the present life and receive bitter retribution in the future.

18. The Parable of Sharpening a Knife at the Pillar (18) The Parable of Sharpening a Knife at the Pillar: Once upon a time, there was a man who, being poor and destitute, worked for a king. As many days and months passed, his body became emaciated and weak.
The king, moved by compassion, granted him a dead camel.

Having received it, the poor man immediately began to skin it; because he found his knife to be dull, he sought a stone to sharpen it. He then found a whetstone on the upper floor of the palace, sharpened his knife until it was keen, and came down to skin the animal.

Thus, as he went back and forth repeatedly to sharpen his blade, he eventually grew weary and exhausted, finding it too burdensome to climb up again and again; so he suspended the donkey atop the tower and approached the stone from there to sharpen his blade, becoming a great object of ridicule for the multitude.

It is like a fool who violates the precepts, amassing great wealth in hopes of cultivating merit and attaining rebirth in heaven; it is like sharpening a blade on a revolving donkey-mill atop a tower—though the labor expended is immense, the result gained is exceedingly meager.

19. The Parable of Losing a Silver Bowl While Crossing by Boat (19) The Parable of Losing a Silver Bowl While Crossing by Boat: Once, there was a man crossing the sea by boat who lost a silver bowl, which fell into the water.
He immediately thought to himself: "I shall now mark the water with a line; having left it behind, I will retrieve it later."
After traveling for two months, he arrived at the various kingdoms of Siṃhala. Seeing a river, he entered it to search for his lost bowl.
The people asked him, "What do you intend to do?"
He replied,
"I previously lost my ring and now wish to find it. He asked:
"Where was it lost? He replied,
"It was lost upon first entering the sea."
He asked again:
"How long has it been since you lost the sutra?
He replied:
"It has been lost for two months.
He asked, "It has been lost for two months; how is it that you are searching for it now?"
He replied, "When I lost the gong, I made a mark by drawing on the water; the water where I originally drew the mark is no different from this, and for that reason I am searching for it.
He asked again:
"Although the water makes no distinction, when you lost it in the past, it was there; how can you possibly find it now by searching here?
At that time, everyone laughed heartily.

It is also like those of external paths who do not cultivate correct practice; amidst a semblance of goodness, they recklessly calculate suffering and hardship in their pursuit of liberation, just as a fool loses a ring there but searches for it here.

20. The Parable of the Man Who Spoke of the King’s Tyranny (XX) The Parable of the Man Who Spoke of the King’s Tyranny: Once upon a time, there was a man who spoke of the king’s transgressions and faults, saying:
"The king is exceedingly tyrannical and governs without reason."

Upon hearing these words, the king became greatly incensed; without investigating to determine who had actually spoken them, he believed the sycophants and seized a virtuous minister, ordering him to be flayed on the back to yield one hundred *liang* of flesh.

When someone testified that these words were untrue, the king’s heart was filled with remorse; he sought a thousand *liang* of flesh to mend his spine, and throughout the night he groaned with extreme suffering.
When the king heard his voice, he asked, "Why are you so distressed?
I will give you ten times a hundred taels for it; is your mind still not satisfied?"
"Why are you so distressed?
A bystander replied,
"Great King!"

"It is like cutting off a son's head: though one were to obtain a thousand heads, the son’s death cannot be avoided; though one were to obtain ten times more flesh, the pain and suffering cannot be avoided.

It is the same with fools: they do not fear the next world, but out of craving for present pleasure, they oppress sentient beings and conscript the common people to acquire great wealth, hoping thereby to extinguish their sins and obtain meritorious retribution.

For example, it is as impossible as for that king to cut through a person’s spine and take their flesh, then patch the wound with other flesh in the hope of making it painless—such a thing cannot exist.
21. The Parable of the Woman Seeking Another Son (21) In times past, there was a woman who already had one son but desired another.
She asked other women, “Who has the means to enable me to have a son again?”
An old woman said to this wife, "I can cause you to obtain a son through your seeking; however, you must perform a sacrifice to Heaven.
She then asked the old woman:
"What is required for the sacrifice?
the old woman said:
"Slay your son and take his blood to offer to Heaven; then you will surely obtain many children."
At that time, the woman followed those words and intended to kill her son.
A wise person nearby mocked and reviled her, saying:
"How foolish and ignorant you are, to reach such an extreme!"
"Can one who has not yet fathered a son ever obtain it?
Yet he kills his existing son.
So too is the fool: for the sake of pleasure that has not yet arisen, he throws himself into a pit of fire, harming his body in various ways in order to attain rebirth in heaven.
The Sutra of One Hundred Parables, Volume One. Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove of Kalandakanivāpa, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and the eight classes of beings, numbering thirty-six thousand people.
At that time, there were five hundred heterodox brahmins in the assembly who rose from their seats and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We have heard that the Way of the Buddha is vast and profound, beyond the reach of others; therefore we have come to seek instruction. We only pray that you will explain it to us."
The Buddha said, "Excellent. He asked:
"Is the world existent or non-existent?
He replied:
"It is both existent and non-existent."
The brahmin said:
"If it exists now, why do you say it does not?
If it does not exist now, why do you say it does?"
He replied:
"The living say 'it exists,' while the dead say 'it does not exist'; therefore, I speak of it as both existing and non-existing. He asked:
“From what are humans born?
He replied,
“Humans are born from grain.”
Question: "From what do the five grains arise? Answer:
"The five grains arise from the four great elements, fire, and wind.
He asked: "From what do the four great elements, fire, and wind arise?"
He replied,
"The four great elements— fire and wind— arise from space. He asked:
"From what does emptiness arise?
He replied:
"It arises from non-existence."
Question: "From what does 'non-existence' arise? Answer:
"It arises from spontaneity (*svabhāva*). He asked:
"From what does spontaneity arise?"
He replied:
"It arises from nirvāṇa. He asked:
“From what does nirvāṇa arise?
The Buddha said,
“Why is the matter you now ask about so profound?”
"Nirvana is the dharma that is neither born nor dies.
He asked: "Has the Buddha entered Nirvana yet?"
He replied,
“I have not yet entered nirvāṇa.
[The other asked,] “If you have not yet entered nirvāṇa, how can you know that nirvāṇa is eternal bliss?”
The Buddha said, "I now ask you:
Are the sentient beings in the world suffering or happy?
He replied:
“Sentient beings are in great suffering.
The Buddha asked,
“What is called suffering?”
He replied, "I see that when sentient beings die, their suffering is difficult to endure; therefore, I know the suffering of death.
The Buddha said:
"You are not dead now, yet you know the suffering of death; because I see that the Buddhas of the ten directions are neither born nor die, I know that Nirvana is eternal bliss.
The hearts of the five hundred Brahmacharins opened and their minds were liberated; they requested to receive the five precepts, realized the fruit of Srotapanna, and sat down again as before.
The Buddha said: "Listen well!
I shall now explain many parables for you in detail."

The Parable of Entering the Sea to Fetch Aloeswood (The Parable of Entering the Sea to Fetch Aloeswood). Long ago, there was the son of an elder who entered the sea to fetch aloeswood. After many years had passed, he finally obtained a single cartload and brought it back home.

He went to the market to sell it, but because it was so precious, no one would buy it at all. After many days had passed without being able to sell it, weariness arose in his heart and he became distressed. Seeing others selling charcoal and selling it quickly, he thought to himself:
"It would be better to burn this and make charcoal; thus it can be sold swiftly."
He immediately burned it to charcoal.
He went to the market to sell it, but could not obtain even half a cartload’s worth of its price.

The foolish people of the world are just like this: though they employ immeasurable skillful means and practice with diligent vigor in their aspiration for the fruit of Buddhahood, because it is so difficult to attain, they give rise to a mind of retreat, thinking it better to resolve instead to seek the fruit of a Śrāvaka, swiftly severing birth and death to become an Arhat.

23. The Parable of the Thief Who Steals Brocade to Wrap Old Woolen Cloth (23) The Parable of the Thief Who Steals Brocade to Wrap Old Woolen Cloth: Long ago, there was a thief who entered the house of a wealthy family and stole brocade. He immediately used it to wrap up his old, worn-out woolen cloth and various other belongings, which was laughed at by wise people.

The foolish people of the world are likewise: having already developed faith and entered into the Buddha-dharma, they practice wholesome dharmas and various merits; yet, because of their greed for profit, they destroy their pure precepts and all their merits, becoming objects of ridicule for the world in exactly the same way.

24. The Parable of the Foolish Man Who Roasted Sesame Seeds (24) The Parable of the Foolish Man Who Roasted Sesame Seeds: Once there was a foolish man who found raw sesame seeds unpalatable; however, he found them delicious when roasted.
He then thought to himself, "It would be better to roast them before planting them, so that I may obtain delicious ones later."
He then parched the seeds and planted them, so that they could never again take root.

People of the world are just like this: because the Bodhisattva practiced for kalpas on end and performed difficult and painful austerities, they consider such things unpleasant and think to themselves, "It would be better to become an Arhat;
one can quickly sever birth and death, for its merit is very easy to attain."
"Later, when they seek the fruit of Buddhahood, it can never be attained; like those scorched seeds that have no further possibility of growth, so too are the foolish people of the world.

25. The Parable of Water and Fire (XXV) Once there was a man who required both fire and cold water. He immediately used his kindled fire to heat a bronze basin filled with water and placed it over the flame. Later, when he wished to take the fire, the fire had completely gone out; when he wished to take the cold water, the water was hot. Thus, he lost both things: the fire and the cold water.

People of the world are likewise thus: having entered the Buddha-dharma to leave the household life and seek the Way, once they have left home, they again think of their wives, children, kinsmen, worldly affairs, and the pleasures of the five desires.
For this reason, one loses the fire of merit and the water of ethical discipline; it is the same for a person who dwells on sensual desire. 26.
The Parable of the Man Who Imitated the King’s Blinking (26) Once there was a man who wished to win the favor of a king. He asked others, "How can I achieve this?"
Someone said to him, "If you wish to win the king's favor, you should imitate the king's physical appearance.
Thereupon, the man went to the king's presence; seeing the king's eyes twitch, he immediately imitated the king's twitching.
The king asked him, saying,
"Are you ill? Or are you afflicted by wind?"
"Why do your eyes twitch?
The man replied to the king, "My eyes are not diseased, nor am I afflicted by wind; I wished to capture Your Majesty's favor, and seeing that Your Majesty’s eyes were twitching, I imitated you."
Upon hearing these words, the king became greatly incensed and immediately dispatched men to inflict various forms of harm upon him and banish him from the country.
It is the same with worldly people: though they wish to draw near to the Buddha, the King of Dharma, and seek his wholesome teachings for their own growth, [they act otherwise].

Having gained access to him, they fail to understand that the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, manifests various forms of deficiency through skillful means for the sake of sentient beings; instead, upon hearing his teachings or seeing that certain words and phrases appear incorrect, they immediately give rise to derision and disparagement, imitating what is improper.
For this reason, within the Buddha-dharma they will forever lose their goodness and fall into the three evil realms; they are just like that man who followed the king’s example. 27.

The Parable of Healing a Laceration from a Whip (Twenty-seven). Once there was a man who was whipped by a king. Having been whipped, he applied horse dung to the wound, wishing for it to heal quickly.
A foolish man, seeing this, felt joy arise in his heart and said to himself:
"I shall certainly obtain this method for treating wounds.
He then returned home and spoke to his son, saying:
"I shall have you lash my back so that I may test the excellent Dharma I have received.
The son then lashed his back and massaged it with horse dung, considering this to be a skillful method.

People of the world are likewise: when they hear someone say that by practicing the contemplation of impurity one can immediately eliminate the sores of the five aggregates, they will say, "I wish to contemplate female beauty and the five desires."
Failing to see impurity, they are instead deluded and distracted by female beauty; thus they wander through birth and death and fall into the hells, and so it is with the foolish people of the world.

28. The Parable of Trading the Wife’s Nose (28) The Parable of Trading the Wife’s Nose: Once there was a man whose wife was beautiful, except that her nose was ugly. When the man went out and saw another woman whose face was beautiful and whose nose was very fine, he thought to himself:
"Would it not be well for me now to cut off her nose and place it upon my wife's face?"
He immediately cut off the nose of another woman’s wife and brought it home, urgently calling out to his own wife:
"Come out quickly; I shall give you a fine nose.

When the wife came out, he cut off her own nose and promptly placed the other woman's nose upon her face. However, as it would not adhere, he lost that nose as well, having caused his wife to suffer great agony in vain.

The foolish people of the world are also like this: when they hear that certain long-established śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas possess great fame and virtue, and are honored by the world to receive great offerings and sustenance, they immediately think to themselves:
"I am now no different from them."
To falsely assume a name for oneself and deceitfully claim to possess virtue is to lose both one's profit and harm one's conduct.
It is like cutting off another's nose only to wound oneself; the foolish people of the world are just like this.

29. The Parable of the Poor Man Burning His Coarse Woolen Garment (29) The Parable of the Poor Man Burning His Coarse Woolen Garment: Once upon a time, there was a man who was impoverished and destitute. He worked as a laborer for others and received a coarse woolen garment, which he wore.
Someone saw him and said to him:
"You are of noble lineage, the son of a dignified person; why do you wear these coarse and tattered garments?
I shall now instruct you so that you may obtain exquisite and superior clothing; follow my words and I will never deceive you."

The poor man joyfully and respectfully followed his words; the man immediately lit a fire in front of him and said to the poor man, "Now you may take off this coarse woolen garment and cast it into the fire;
at this place of burning, I shall cause you to obtain a most excellent and precious robe."
The poor man immediately took off his garment and threw it into the fire; once it was burned, he searched for it at that spot of fire but found nothing at all. People of the world are just like this:

having attained this human body by practicing various wholesome dharmas through their past lives, they ought to protect it, advance in virtue, and cultivate their deeds. Yet they are deceived by external paths, evil ones, and seductive women who say:

"You should now believe my words and practice various ascetic penances; after casting yourself from cliffs or leaping into fires and abandoning this body, you shall be born in the Brahma Heaven and enjoy happiness forever."

He then followed those words and immediately sacrificed his life; after his death, he fell into hell and underwent all manner of sufferings. Having lost his human body without gaining anything at all, he was just like that poor man.

30. The Parable of the Shepherd (Thirty) The Parable of the Shepherd: Once there was a man who was skilled at tending sheep. His flock grew so large that it numbered in the millions. Yet, being exceedingly stingy and greedy, he was unwilling to spend anything on external things.
At that time, there was a man skilled in artifice who, employing a stratagem, went to visit a close friend and said to him:
"I am now so deeply bound by affection with you that we have become as one body, no different from each other."
"I know that family has a beautiful daughter; I shall seek her for you to be your wife.
Upon hearing this, the shepherd was filled with joy and gave him many sheep and various other riches.
The man spoke again:
"Your wife has given birth to a son today.
Although the shepherd had not yet seen his wife, upon hearing that she had given birth, his heart was filled with great joy, and he gave him even more goods.
Later, that man returned and said to him,
"Your son was born, but now he has died.
Upon hearing these words, the shepherd wept aloud, sobbing and lamenting without ceasing.

The people of the world are likewise in this regard: having cultivated much learning, they harbor their teachings in secret for the sake of fame and profit, refusing to teach or explain them to others; thus, they are deceived and deluded by this defiled body, falsely anticipating worldly pleasures.

Just as when one is deceived by one's own wife or children, loses wholesome qualities, and subsequently loses both body and life along with wealth, one weeps with great compassion and gives rise to sorrow and suffering; so too it is for that shepherd.
31. The Parable of Hiring a Potter (31) The Parable of Hiring a Potter: Once there was a Brahmin teacher who intended to hold a great assembly.
He said to his disciple, "I require earthenware vessels for the use of the assembly; you should hire a potter for me and go to the market to find one."
Then that disciple went to the house of a potter.

At that time, there was a man who had loaded donkeys with earthenware vessels and was going to the market to sell them; in a short while, the donkeys broke all the vessels. Returning home, they wept and wailed in distress.
Having seen this, the disciple asked him, "Why do you lament and suffer such distress?"

The man replied, "Through diligent effort and hardship over many years, I have finally succeeded in crafting this vessel. I was going to the market to sell it when this wretched donkey, in a mere instant, completely smashed my vessel; that is why I am so distressed."
At that time, having seen and heard this, the disciple was delighted and said:
"This donkey is truly a fine thing; what it has accomplished over a long period of time it can now destroy in an instant. I shall purchase this donkey."
The potter was delighted and immediately sold it to him.
When he returned home riding it, his teacher asked him, "Why did you not have the potter bring it? What use have you for this donkey?"
The disciple replied, "This donkey is superior to the potter; what the potter has spent a long time crafting, this donkey can shatter in a short moment.
Then the teacher said to him:
"You are greatly foolish and devoid of wisdom! This donkey can only just now be broken; even if one were to spend a hundred years, it could not be accomplished.

People of the world are just like this: though they receive offerings for a thousand or ten thousand years, they provide no recompense at all; they constantly cause harm and never bring benefit. Those who betray kindness are likewise so.
32. The Parable of the Merchant Who Stole Gold Once upon a time, there were two merchants who traveled together on a trading journey. One sold genuine gold, while the second sold *tūla* cotton.

There was another who wished to buy genuine gold and tested it by burning it; meanwhile, a second merchant immediately stole that burnt gold and wrapped it in *tūla* cotton. Because the gold was still hot, it completely consumed the cotton; once the situation was revealed, he lost both his wits and his goods.

Just as those non-Buddhists stole the Buddha-dharma and incorporated it into their own teachings, falsely claiming it was their own and not the Buddha-dharma, so too, by this means, the external scriptures were burned and ceased to circulate in the world; the entire matter was revealed just like the theft of gold. It is exactly like that.

33. The Parable of Cutting Down a Tree to Gather Fruit (33) The Parable of Cutting Down a Tree to Gather Fruit: Long ago, there was a king who had a magnificent tree, exceedingly tall and vast, which produced superior fruit that was fragrant and sweet.
At that time, a man came to where the king was, and the king said to him, "On this tree, beautiful fruit is about to grow; can you eat it?
He immediately replied to the king:
"This tree is so tall and broad; even if I wished to eat its fruit, by what means could I possibly obtain it?

He then cut down the tree in hopes of reaching its fruit, but having gained nothing, he merely exhausted himself in vain. Later, wishing to set it upright again, he found the tree already withered and dead, with no possibility of life remaining.

The people of the world are also like this. The Tathāgata, the Dharma King, possesses the tree of precepts that can produce superior fruit. If one gives rise to the aspiration and desire to obtain its fruit, one ought to maintain the precepts and cultivate various merits. Yet, failing to understand the skillful means, they instead destroy their own prohibitions—just as one who cuts down a tree and then wishes for it to live again can never achieve it; so too it is with those who break the precepts.

34. The Parable of Sending Fine Water (34). The Parable of Sending Fine Water: Once there was a village located five yojanas from the royal capital, and within that village there was excellent, fine water.
The king commanded the villagers to provide him with fine water every day; the villagers became exhausted and distressed, and all wished to move away from this village to a distant place.
At that time, the headman of the village said to the people: "Do not go!
"I shall petition the King on your behalf to reduce the distance from five yojanas to three yojanas, so that you may travel back and forth without fatigue.
He then went to inform the King, who reduced it to three yojanas. Upon hearing this, the multitude was filled with great joy.
Someone said to him, "This is indeed the original five *yojanas*; there is no difference at all.
Although he heard these words, because he trusted the king’s speech, he ultimately refused to abandon his position.

People of the world are also like this: though they practice the True Dharma to cross over the five realms of existence toward the city of Nirvāṇa, their minds become weary and exhausted, and they wish to abandon it; they halt their carriage within saṃsāra and can no longer advance.

The Tathāgata, the Dharma King, possesses great skillful means; within the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna), he distinguishes and teaches three vehicles. When followers of the Lesser Vehicle hear this, they rejoice, considering it easy to practice; they cultivate goodness, advance in virtue, and seek deliverance from birth and death. Later, when they hear others say that there are no three vehicles and that there is but a single path, [they are led to realize the ultimate truth].
Because he believed the Buddha’s words, he was ultimately unwilling to abandon them; the man from that village was just like this. 35.

The Parable of the Mirror in a Precious Casket (XXXV) Once upon a time, there was a man who was impoverished and destitute. He owed many people debts which he had no means to repay, so he fled into a desolate wilderness.
He encountered a chest filled with precious jewels, upon which a bright mirror was placed as a lid.
Upon seeing this, the poor man was filled with great joy and immediately opened it; however, when he saw his own reflection in the mirror, he was struck with terror and joined his palms, saying:
"I thought this was an empty chest containing nothing at all, not knowing that you were here within it; please do not be angry with me."

Ordinary worldlings are also like this: they are beset by immeasurable afflictions and entangled by the creditors of the Māra-king of birth and death; yet, wishing to escape birth and death, they enter into the Buddha-dharma to practice wholesome dharmas and cultivate various meritorious virtues.

It is like encountering a precious casket, yet being deluded and distracted by the mirror of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi). Falsely perceiving a self, one becomes attached to it, claiming it to be real; consequently, one falls away and loses all merits—the meditative concentrations, the factors of enlightenment, the untainted virtues, and the fruits of the paths of the Three Vehicles—all are utterly lost.
Just as that foolish man discarded the casket of jewels, so too is it with those who cling to the view of a self.

36. The Parable of the Five-Supernormal-Power Seer’s Eye (36): The Parable of the Five-Supernormal-Power Seer’s Eye. Once there was a man who entered the mountains to study the Way and became a seer possessing the five supernormal powers. With his divine eye, he could see through all things and perceive every kind of hidden treasure buried within the earth.
Upon hearing this, the king was greatly delighted and said to his ministers,
"How can we ensure that this man remains forever in my kingdom and does not go elsewhere?"
"May my treasury be filled with many rare treasures.
A foolish minister immediately went there, gouged out both of the seer's eyes, and brought them back to report to the king:
"I have gouged out his eyes; he can no longer leave, but shall remain in this kingdom forever."

The king said to his minister, "The reason I desired to have the rishi dwell here was so that he might see all the hidden treasures beneath the earth; now that you have destroyed his eyes, what further use is he?"

People of the world are likewise: seeing others practicing asceticism (dhūta), performing austerities in mountains, forests, wildernesses, among graves, or beneath trees, cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā), they forcibly bring them to their own homes and provide various offerings. They thus destroy the other's wholesome dharmas, causing the fruits of the Path to fail to be realized and the eye of the Path to be lost. Having already forfeited the benefit, they obtain nothing at all, just like that foolish minister who pointlessly destroyed the eyes of another.

37. The Parable of Slaying a Herd of Cattle (37) The Parable of Slaying a Herd of Cattle: Once upon a time, there was a man who possessed two hundred and fifty head of cattle. He would constantly drive them to water and pasture, feeding them according to the seasons.
At that time, there was a tiger that had devoured one ox. Then the owner of the ox immediately thought to himself:
"I have already lost one ox and am no longer complete; what use is this remaining ox?"
They immediately drove them to the edge of a deep pit and cast them into the bottom, killing them all.

Foolish ordinary people are just like this: though they receive and uphold the complete precepts of the Tathāgata, if they violate even a single precept, they feel no shame and do not perform a pure confession; instead, they think to themselves:
"I have already broken one precept; since it is no longer complete, what is the use of upholding the rest?"
"Everything is destroyed so that not a single thing remains, just as when that foolish man slaughtered the entire herd of oxen until not one remained. 38.

The Parable of Drinking Water from a Wooden Tube (38) Once upon a time, there was a man who, while traveling, became weary and thirsty. Seeing clear, flowing water within a wooden tube, he approached it and drank. Having drunk his fill, he immediately raised his hand and said to the wooden tube:
"I have finished drinking; let no more water come forth."
Although he spoke these words, the flow of water continued as before; thereupon, he spoke with anger:
"I have already finished drinking and told you not to come; for what reason have you come?"
Someone saw him and said:
"You are utterly foolish and devoid of wisdom!
Why do you not leave, instead telling me not to come?"
He immediately pulls it back and leads it elsewhere.

People of the world are just like this: driven by the thirst of birth and death, they drink the brackish water of the five desires. Once they have grown weary and satiated by those five desires—just as that elephant was when its thirst was quenched—they say:
"O forms, sounds, scents, and tastes, do not come before me again to be seen."
However, these five desires continued without interruption; having seen them, he again became angry and said:
"Tell them to extinguish themselves quickly and not arise again! Why have they come so that I must see them?"
At that time, a wise man spoke to him, saying:
"If you wish to attain liberation, you should restrain your six sense-faculties and close off the mind and its intentions; when delusive thoughts do not arise, you will then attain emancipation."
"Why must you not see it? Why do you wish to prevent its arising?
This is no different from the foolish man who drank the water. 39.

The Parable of Seeing Another’s Plastered House (39) The Parable of Seeing Another’s Plastered House: Once there was a man who went to another’s house. He saw that the walls of the house were plastered and treated, and that the floor was level, clean, and very beautiful. He then asked him, saying:
"What did you mix with the plaster to make it so beautiful?
The host replied, "I soaked rice husks in water until they were soft, then mixed them with mud to coat the walls; that is how it became like this."
The foolish man then thought to himself:
"If I use only rice husks, it will not be as good; I should mix them with rice grains so that the wall may be white and pure, and the plastering smooth and fine."
He then used rice grains mixed with mud to coat his walls, hoping to make them level and smooth; instead, they became even more uneven, and the walls split apart entirely.
The rice was wasted in vain without any benefit; it would have been better to give it away in charity to gain merit.

Ordinary people are just like this: hearing the Dharma preached by the sages and practicing various virtues, they think that after casting off this body they will be reborn in heaven or attain liberation; yet they then take their own lives in the hope of attaining heaven or liberation. In vain they waste themselves and achieve nothing at all, just like those foolish men.

40. The Parable of Treating Baldness (40) The Parable of Treating Baldness: Once upon a time, there was a man who had no hair on his head. In winter he suffered from the great cold, and in summer he was afflicted by heat; furthermore, he was bitten by mosquitoes and gadflies, enduring distress day and night, which he found to be extremely painful.
There was a physician skilled in many medical arts; at that time, the bald man went to his place and said to the physician, "I pray only that you, Great Master, will treat me."
At that time, the physician was also bald; he immediately removed his cap, showed him his head, and said to him:
"I too suffer from this and find it painful. If you can cure me when I treat you, you should first treat yourself to eliminate your own affliction."

The people of the world are likewise thus: afflicted by birth, old age, sickness, and death, they seek a place of long life and immortality. Hearing that there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who are the world’s excellent physicians, skillfully treating all ailments, they go to them and say:
"I pray only that you will remove for me this affliction of impermanent birth and death, so that I may dwell forever in peace and happiness, existing eternally and unchanging."

Then the brahmins and others replied, "We too suffer from this impermanence of birth, old age, sickness, and death; though we have sought everywhere for a place of eternal abiding, in the end we could not find it."
"If I were now able to cause you to obtain it, I should have first obtained it myself so that you might also obtain it.
It is like that person suffering from baldness who merely exhausts himself in vain and cannot achieve a cure.

41. The Parable of the Piśāca Demons (41). Once, there were two piśāca demons who shared one casket, one staff, and one pair of sandals. The two demons quarreled over them, each desiring to possess them for himself; they wrangled throughout the entire day without being able to reach a settlement.
At that time, a man came, saw them, and asked:
"What extraordinary thing is in this chest, staff,
and sandals that you are all so angry and disputing?"
The two spirits replied, "This casket of ours can produce all manner of clothing, food, drink, bedding, furniture, and articles of daily necessity; everything emerges from within it."
"One who wields this staff will have their enemies submit and none dare to contend with them;
one who wears these sandals will be able to fly through the air without obstruction.
Having heard this, the man immediately said to the ghost:
"You two move a little further away; I shall divide it equally for you.
Upon hearing these words, the two ghosts immediately retreated to a distance.
The man instantly took up his basket, grasped his staff, and stepped into his sandals, flying off. The two ghosts were struck with astonishment and ultimately gained nothing.
The human spoke in the language of ghosts, saying:
"I have already resolved the disputes you were engaged in; now I shall cause you to have no further contention.
The *piśācas* are a metaphor for the various Māras and non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
Generosity is like a casket, from which all the requisites for sustenance within the five realms of existence—both human and celestial—emerge.
Meditative concentration is like a staff, with which one subdues the thieves of Māra, enmity, and afflictions.
Maintaining the precepts is like wearing wooden clogs; one will surely ascend to the realms of humans and devas.
As for those who contend over the "box" of demons and external paths, this is a metaphor for forcibly seeking karmic rewards within the tainted states of existence, where one gains nothing at all.
If one can practice wholesome conduct, as well as generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration, one will then be able to leave suffering behind and attain the fruits of the Path.
