42. The Parable of the Caravan’s Dead Camel (The Parable of the Five Hundred Joyful Pills) It is like this:

Suppose there were a merchant traveling abroad on business who, while on the road, suddenly encountered a camel that died. Upon the camel were loaded many precious treasures, as well as various items such as fine, soft, high-quality cotton cloth and other miscellaneous goods.
Once the camel had died, they immediately skinned it. The caravan leader set aside his walking and sitting disciples and said to them, "Take good care of the camel skin;
do not let it become damp or rotten."

Later, when it rained, the two foolish and ignorant men covered this hide entirely with fine cotton cloth; the cloth was completely ruined, for the value of the hide and the cotton cloth are naturally poles apart, yet out of folly they used the cloth to cover the hide.

People of the world are likewise: those who do not kill are likened to white cotton cloth; the camel skins represent their wealth and goods; and the rain that makes them damp and rotten represents negligence that ruins virtuous conduct.

The precept against killing is the supreme and most wondrous cause for the Buddha’s Dharma-body; yet, being unable to cultivate it, people instead use wealth and goods to construct various stupas and temples to make offerings to the Sangha. Thus, they abandon the root to grasp at the branches, failing to seek the fundamental source. Consequently, they drift through the five realms of existence, unable to escape on their own. For this reason, practitioners should maintain the precept against killing with a focused and sincere mind.

43. The Parable of Grinding a Great Stone (43): The Parable of Grinding a Great Stone. For example, suppose there were a person who, exerting great effort upon a large stone, spent months and years carving it into a small toy ox; the labor expended was immense, yet the result expected was trivial.
People of the world are also like this: grinding large stones is a metaphor for the diligent toil of study, while making small oxen is a metaphor for mutual fame and the pursuit of right and wrong.

Now, for one who studies, having investigated with refined thought and attained extensive knowledge and broad learning, it would be appropriate to practice accordingly and seek the supreme fruit from afar; yet, instead, they seek only fame, becoming arrogant and conceited, thereby increasing their faults and afflictions.

44. The Parable of the Half-Cake (44): The Parable of the Half-Cake Suppose there were a person who, because of hunger, ate seven fried cakes. Having eaten six and a half, he became fully satiated. The man felt resentment and regret, striking himself with his hand and saying:
"My present satiety is due to this half-cake; yet the previous six cakes were wasted in vain. Had I known that this half-cake could provide such sufficiency, I should have eaten it first."
The people of the world are likewise: from the very beginning they have never possessed true happiness, yet through delusion and inversion they falsely conceive the notion of pleasure.
Just as that foolish man conceived the thought of satiety from half a loaf of cake, so too do ignorant worldly people regard wealth and status as happiness.

Now, as for wealth and honor: the pursuit of them is extremely bitter; once they have been obtained, guarding them is also bitter; and later, when they are lost, the anxiety over them is again bitter. Throughout these three stages, there is no happiness at all.
Just as clothing and food are called "pleasure" because they provide a covering, one falsely gives rise to the perception of pleasure amidst suffering and toil. The Buddhas have declared:
"There is no peace in the three realms; all are great suffering. It is only through the delusions of ordinary beings that they falsely give rise to the perception of pleasure."
45. The Parable of the Servant Guarding the Gate (45). The Parable of the Servant Guarding the Gate: Suppose there is a man who, intending to travel far away, commands his servant, saying:
"Guard the gate well and look after the donkey's fodder."

After his master had departed, there was a house in the neighborhood where music was being performed. This slave, wishing to listen, could not remain at peace; he immediately tied the door with a rope, placed it upon a donkey, and carried it to the place of entertainment to hear the music.
After the slave had departed, the thief took all the wealth and property from the house.
When the master returned home, he asked the slave,
"Where are the treasures?"
The slave replied, "Master, you previously gave me the gate-ass and the rope; beyond that, it is not within my knowledge.
The master spoke again:
"Leaving you to guard the gate was solely for the sake of wealth; now that the wealth is lost, what use is there in guarding the gate?

It is the same with the foolish people of birth and death who are slaves to craving: the Tathāgata instructs them to constantly guard the gates of the senses, not to cling to the six sense-objects, and to keep watch over the donkey of ignorance while holding the rope of craving.

Yet these bhikṣus do not follow the Buddha’s teachings; greedily seeking gain and offerings, they falsely manifest purity while sitting in secluded places. Their minds wander and race, craving and clinging to the five desires; deluded and distracted by forms, sounds, smells, and tastes, their hearts are shrouded by ignorance and entangled by the snares of craving. Thus, the treasures of right mindfulness, awakening, and the factors of the path are all utterly lost.
46. The Parable of Stealing the Yak (46): The Parable of Stealing the Yak For example, suppose a village collectively steals a yak and eats it together.
The owner of the lost yak tracks its footprints to the village and calls out to the villagers, questioning them about the circumstances and saying to them:
"You are here in this village."
The one who did not steal replied,
“I truly have no village.
He asked again:
“In your village there is a pond; did you eat ox meat together by the side of that pond?
He replied, “There is no pond.”
He asked again,
"Are there trees by the side of the pond?
He replied:
"There are no trees.
He asked again,
"When you stole the ox, was it not to the east of your village?"
He replied, "There is no east.
He asked again:
“Was it not during the midday when you stole the ox?
He replied, “No, it was not.”
He asked again:
"Even if there were no villages and no trees, how could there be a world without the east or without time?
I know your lies are utterly untrustworthy; did you steal the ox and eat it?"
He replied, "I am truly eating.

A person who has broken the precepts is just like this: concealing their transgressions and refusing to confess them, they enter hell at death. The devas and benevolent spirits, observing with their divine eyes, cannot allow such concealment; it is just as that ox-eater could not deceive or resist [the consequences].

47. The Parable of the Poor Man Making the Cry of a Mandarin Duck (47) The Parable of the Poor Man Making the Cry of a Mandarin Duck: Once, on the day of a national festival in a foreign land, all the women wore *utpala* flowers as their floral ornaments.
There was a poor man whose wife said to him:
"If you can obtain an *utpala* flower and bring it to me, I will remain your wife;
if you cannot obtain one, I shall abandon you and depart."
Her husband, who had previously been skilled at imitating the cries of a ruddy sheldrake, entered the royal pond and made the cry of a ruddy sheldrake while stealing blue lotuses.
At that time, the pond-keeper asked:
"Who is in the pond?"
Then this poor man, losing his composure, replied:
"I am a ruddy sheldrake.
The guards seized him and took him to the king's presence; yet on the way, he again sang in harmony, making the cry of a ruddy sheldrake. The keepers of the pond said:
"If you did not do so previously, what benefit is there in doing it now?

So too it is with the foolish people of the world: throughout their entire lives they commit various evil deeds through violence and harm, yet they do not practice mental cultivation to bring the mind under control;
only when facing the end of life do they say, "Now I wish to cultivate goodness."

The hell-wardens lead him away to deliver him to King Yama; though he wishes to cultivate goodness, it is already too late. He is like that foolish man who, wishing to reach the king’s palace, let out the cry of a ruddy sheldrake.

48. The Parable of the Jackal Struck by a Falling Tree Branch (48) The Parable of the Jackal Struck by a Falling Tree Branch: Suppose, for example, there was a jackal beneath a tree. When the wind blew and a branch broke and fell upon its back, it immediately closed its eyes, unwilling to look at the tree. It abandoned the spot and fled to an open field, refusing to return even until sunset.
Seeing from afar the wind blowing through the branches and twigs of a great tree, causing them to sway up and down, one might say it was calling for him and immediately go beneath the tree.

A foolish disciple is just like this: having already left the household life and come close to his preceptor, he flees at the mere sound of a slight reprimand; yet later, encountering evil associates who trouble him incessantly, he returns to where he had gone. Such coming and going is what constitutes folly and delusion.

49. The Parable of the Two Children Disputing over Hairs (49) The Parable of the Two Children Disputing over Hairs: For example, in the past, two children went into a river to play. There, at the bottom of the water, they found a handful of hair.
One child said, "This is the beard of a seer."
One of the young boys said, "This is bear fur.
At that time, there was a rishi by the river; as the two boys continued to dispute without ceasing, they went to the rishi's dwelling to resolve their doubt.
The seer immediately took some rice and sesame seeds, chewed them in his mouth, and spat them into his palm, saying to the boy:
"What is in my palm resembles peacock droppings."
It was well known that this seer did not answer the questions posed to him.

In the same way, foolish people of the world likewise engage in frivolous discourse regarding various phenomena rather than answering according to correct principle when the Dharma is being taught; like that seer who failed to answer what was asked, they become objects of derision for all people, and their superficial, empty talk is just the same.

50. The Parable of Treating a Hunchback (Fifty) The Parable of Treating a Hunchback: Suppose there was a man who suddenly fell ill with a hunched back and invited a physician to treat him. The physician applied ghee and placed wooden boards above and below his body, pressing down with great force. Unaware of what was happening, the man’s two eyes were both forced out at once.

The foolish people of the world are likewise: for the sake of cultivating merit, they engage in various unrighteous acts such as managing livelihoods through trade and commerce; though their undertakings succeed, the profit does not compensate for the harm, and in future lives they enter hell, like eyes being gouged out.
51. The Parable of Five Men Buying a Maidservant and Employing Her Together (51) The Parable of Five Men Buying a Maidservant and Employing Her Together: Suppose five men together buy a maidservant.
One among them says to this maidservant, "Wash my clothes."
Next, another person spoke again to the washerwoman.
The maidservant said to that person:
"Wash his clothes first."
The latter one said in anger, "I purchased [this] from you at the same time as the person before me; why do you treat me alone in this way?
He then struck him ten times with a whip. In this manner, each of the five men struck him ten times.

The five aggregates are likewise: through the causal conditions of afflictions, this body is composed; yet these five aggregates constantly torment sentient beings with the immeasurable sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death.

52. The Parable of the Entertainer Playing Music (52) The Parable of the Entertainer Playing Music: It is as if an entertainer were performing music before a king, and the king granted him a thousand coins.
Later, he requested [the money] from the king, but the king would not give it to him, saying to him:
"Just now you provided music and merely amused my ears; I gave you the money merely to amuse yours."

The karmic rewards of the world are likewise thus: although one may experience slight pleasure among humans or in the heavens, it possesses no reality; being impermanent and subject to decay and destruction, it cannot endure for long, just like that empty pleasure.

53. The Parable of the Teacher Suffering from a Foot and Entrusting His Two Disciples For example, there was a teacher who had two disciples. The teacher suffered from a foot ailment and sent his two disciples away, instructing each to take turns massaging one of his feet at the appropriate times.
The two disciples were constantly hostile toward one another. When one disciple went out, the other seized the leg he was meant to massage and broke it with a stone;
when the first returned, he was enraged by this and likewise seized the leg his companion had been massaging and immediately broke it as well.

The disciples of the Buddha’s Dharma are likewise thus: those who study the Vaipulya do not disparage the Hīnayāna, and those who study the Hīnayāna likewise do not disparage the Vaipulya; yet, because of this, both paths of the Great Sage’s scriptural canon have been lost.

54. The Parable of the Snake’s Head and Tail Contending for Precedence (54) The parable of the snake’s head and tail contending for precedence is as follows: Suppose there were a snake, and the tail said to the head, "I should go in front."
The head said to the tail, "I am always in front; why have you suddenly done this?

Indeed, the head was in front, while the tail became entangled in a tree and could not move forward. When it let go of the tail and moved forward, it immediately fell into a pit of fire, being scorched and burned to death.
It is the same for teachers and their disciples: the teacher, being elderly, always remains at the front, while we, being young, should act as the leaders.
Thus, these youths, unacquainted with the precepts and committing many transgressions, are subsequently led one after another into hell.

55. The Parable of the Barber Who Wished to Shave the King’s Beard In the past, there was a king who had a trusted attendant. During a military engagement, this man risked his life to save the king, ensuring his safety. The king was greatly delighted and granted him whatever he wished for, asking immediately:
"What do you seek?"
"Do as you wish," [the king] said.
The minister then replied,
"When Your Majesty shaves your beard, I pray that you will allow me to shave it as well."
The king said,
"If this matter suits your wishes, I grant you your request. Thus,
though such a fool is laughed at by the world— where he could have obtained the governance of half the kingdom and the position of chief minister— he instead seeks a menial occupation.

Fools are likewise so: though the Buddhas, over immeasurable kalpas, attained Buddhahood through difficult practices and asceticism, if one encounters a Buddha or meets with the bequeathed Dharma, such a human body is as difficult to obtain as a blind turtle encountering the hole of a floating wooden plank. These two rare opportunities have now been met; yet their resolve is inferior, for they consider it sufficient to observe a few precepts and do not seek the supreme and wondrous Dharma of Nirvana. Lacking the intention to strive forward, they perform only perverse deeds and consider these sufficient.

56. The Parable of the Rope and Nothingness (56): The Parable of the Rope and Nothingness. Once, two men were traveling together on a road when they saw another man leading a cart loaded with sesame seeds who was unable to proceed along a perilous path.
Then the driver said to the two men,
"Help me push this cart out of this dangerous path.
The two replied:
"What will you give me? the driver said,
"I have nothing to give you."
Then these two men immediately assisted in pushing the cart until it reached level ground, and said to the driver:
"Give us our share. He replied:
"Nothing," he said;
and again he spoke, saying,
"Give me nothing."
Between the two, one of them spoke with a smile, saying:
"He was unwilling to give it; why should that be a cause for grief?
The other person replied:
"If there is nothing given to me, there must necessarily be 'nothing'.
Another person said:
"'Nothing' is a conventional designation formed by the combination of two characters."

If worldly ordinary persons perceive that there is no thing, they give rise to the sphere of nothingness; as for the second person who says there is no thing, this refers to the signless, the wishless, and the unconditioned.
57. The Parable of Treading on the Elder’s Mouth (57). Once there was a wealthy elder whose attendants, wishing to please him, treated him with the utmost reverence.
When the elder spat, his attendants on the left and right stepped upon it with their feet.
There was one foolish man who did not manage to step upon it in time and spoke these words:
"If people step upon what is spat on the ground, then when I am about to spit, I shall step upon it first."
Thereupon, just as the elder was about to cough or spit, this foolish man immediately raised his foot and kicked the elder’s mouth, splitting his lips and breaking his teeth.
The elder said to the foolish man,
"Why did you kick my lips and mouth?"

The fool replied, "If the elder spits from his mouth and it falls to the ground, those sycophants on his left and right have already stepped over and removed it; though I wish to step over it as well, I am always unable to catch up."
"For this reason, when saliva is about to escape from the mouth, one raises the foot first to kick it away, hoping thereby to fulfill one's intention.

All things require their proper time; if the time has not yet arrived and one forcibly exerts effort, one instead incurs suffering. For this reason, people of the world should know the difference between the timely and the untimely."

58. The Parable of the Two Sons Dividing Their Wealth (58) The Parable of the Two Sons Dividing Their Wealth: Long ago, in the kingdom of Malla, there was a Kṣatriya who fell gravely ill. Knowing for certain that he would die, he instructed his two sons:
“After my death, divide my wealth and property well.”
The two sons followed these instructions and divided the estate into two portions after his death; however, the elder brother claimed that the younger brother’s share was unfair.
At that time, there was an old fool who said:
"I shall teach you how to divide the property so that it becomes equal."
He divided all his possessions into two portions. How did he divide them?
He cut his clothes down the middle into two parts;

he likewise broke his bowls and jars down the middle into two parts; he also broke all his large and small jars into two parts; and he even broke his coins into two parts. In this manner, he divided every single possession he had entirely into two portions.

Distributing property in such a manner was ridiculed by others, much like the various non-Buddhist outsiders who exclusively cultivate the *vibhajya-vāda* (analytical method). There are four types of analytical methods (*vibhaṅga-mukha*):
the analytical method of categorical response (*ekāṃśa-vyākaraṇa*), for example, when one says that all who exist must die; this is the analytical method of categorical response.

"The deceased must necessarily be reborn" is a question to be answered by way of analysis (*vibhajya-vyākaraṇa*): for one whose craving is exhausted there is no rebirth, whereas for one who possesses craving there is necessarily rebirth. This is called the method of answering by way of analysis.
If someone asks, "Is man the most excellent?
one should reply with a counter-question:
"Are you asking about the three evil realms?"
If one asks about the various heavens,
or if one asks about the three evil realms, humans are truly the most excellent;
but if one asks among the various heavens, humans are certainly inferior.
Such meanings as these are called the *paripṛcchā-vyākaraṇa-mukha* (the method of answering by counter-question).

If one asks about the fourteen difficult questions (*caturdaśa-avyākṛta*), or asks whether the world and sentient beings are finite or infinite, have a beginning and end or no beginning and end, and so forth—such meanings are called the *sthāpanīya-vyākaraṇa-mukha* (the method of answering by setting aside).

The various heterodox teachers, being foolish yet imagining themselves wise, destroy the fourfold system of discourse to establish a single-particularized discourse; this is like a fool dividing money and goods by breaking a coin into two pieces.

59. The Parable of Observing the Making of a Jar (59): The Parable of Observing the Making of a Jar. For example, two people went to a potter’s workshop and watched him tread the wheel to fashion an earthen jar; they gazed upon it without weariness.
One person left and went to a great assembly where he obtained exquisite food and acquired rare treasures;
the other person looked at the jar and said,
"Wait until I have finished looking."
In this manner, as time gradually passed until sunset, he watched the jar incessantly and neglected his food and clothing.
So too it is with the foolish person: they attend to their household affairs and fail to perceive impermanence.
Today one busies oneself with this matter, tomorrow one creates that karma;
when the Great Dragons, the Buddhas, emerge, their thunderous voice pervades the world and the rain of Dharma falls without obstruction, yet due to worldly affairs, one does not hear it.
Not knowing that death has suddenly arrived, One misses this assembly of all Buddhas;
Failing to obtain the precious treasure of the Dharma, One dwells forever in the exhaustion of the evil realms.
Having turned one's back on and abandoned the True Dharma, One contemplates the vessel of conditioned phenomena.
Since it is ultimately and eternally without end, one thus loses the benefit of the Dharma and shall never have a time of liberation.

(60) The Parable of Seeing the Reflection of Gold at the Bottom of Water: Once there was a foolish man who went to a great pond. Seeing the reflection of a true golden image at the bottom of the water, he thought there was gold there; he immediately entered the water and stirred up the mud in search of it.
Exhausted and unable to find it, he came out and sat down again.
After a short while, the water cleared and once more revealed a golden color; he entered further inside and stirred up the mud to search for it again, yet still found nothing.
It being thus, the father sought his son, found him, and upon seeing him, asked:
"What have you been doing that you are so exhausted?
The son replied to his father:
“There is pure gold at the bottom of the water; at that time, I plunged into the water wishing to stir up the mud to retrieve it, but I became utterly exhausted and could not find it.

The father looked at the reflection of the pure gold at the bottom of the water and knew that this gold was actually upon the tree; he knew this because its reflection appeared at the bottom of the water.
His father said,
"It must have been a flying bird that carried gold and placed it upon this tree.
Following his father's words, he climbed the tree and found it.
Ordinary people who are foolish and ignorant, lacking wisdom, are just like this:
within the aggregates that are devoid of self, they perversely give rise to the notion of a self;
just as one who sees the reflection of gold exerts great effort and undergoes hardship in search of it.
61. The Parable of the Disciple of Brahmā Creating Things (61). The assembly of brahmins all said:
"The Great Brahmā King is the father of the world; he is able to create all things."
The Lord of All Creations had a disciple who said, "I too can create all things. This was truly foolishness, for he claimed to possess wisdom.
He spoke to Brahmā, saying, "I wish to create all things."
Brahmādeva said to him, "Do not harbor such a thought; you are not capable of creating.
Yet, disregarding Brahmā’s words, he still desired to create.
When Brahmā saw the object created by his disciple, he spoke to him, saying:

"You have made the head too large and the neck too small; you have made the hands too large and the arms too small; you have made the feet too small and the heels too large; you have made it to resemble a piśāca ghost."

By this principle it should be known that each thing is created by its own respective karma; it is not Brahmā who can create them. The Buddhas teach the Dharma without adhering to the two extremes—neither adhering to annihilationism nor adhering to eternalism—teaching the Dharma in accordance with the Eightfold Noble Path.

Having perceived the views of annihilationism and eternalism, the various non-Buddhists give rise to attachment; they deceive the world by creating formal images and performing rituals, yet what they preach is truly not the Dharma.
62. The Parable of the Sick Man Eating Pheasant Meat Once there was a man whose illness became extremely grave. A skilled physician examined him and declared:
"He must constantly eat a specific kind of pheasant meat to be able to recover from his illness."
The patient had purchased a pheasant in the market and, having eaten it all, did not eat anything else.
Later, when the physician saw him, he asked:
"Has your illness been cured?"
The patient replied, "The physician previously instructed me to eat pheasant meat constantly; therefore, having now finished eating one pheasant, I do not dare to eat another."
The physician spoke again, saying:
"If the pheasants you previously had were already exhausted, why did you not eat more?
How can you hope to recover from your illness by eating only a single pheasant now?"

"All non-Buddhists are likewise thus. When they hear the words of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—the unsurpassed physicians—who say that one must understand consciousness (*vijñāna*), these non-Buddhists, who cling to the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*), claim that the past, future, and present are merely a single consciousness that undergoes no transition or change. This is like eating only a single pheasant; therefore, they cannot cure the disease of their delusion and afflictions."

The Buddhas of Great Wisdom teach all non-Buddhists to eliminate their view of permanence; since all phenomena arise and perish from moment to moment, how could there be a single consciousness that is eternal and unchanging?

Just as that worldly physician instructed [the patient] to eat pheasant meat to recover from his illness, so too does the Buddha instruct all sentient beings to attain liberation: because all phenomena disintegrate, they are not eternal; because they continue, they are not annihilated. Thus, one immediately eradicates the disease of the view of permanence.

63. The Parable of the Actors Wearing Rākṣasa Costumes Who Terrify One Another (63) Once, in the kingdom of Gandhāra, there were some actors who, due to a famine, wandered to other lands in search of food. As they passed through Mount Vāraṇa, they encountered many malevolent spirits and man-eating rākṣasas who had long inhabited that mountain.

At that time, some performers were staying overnight in the mountains; as it was cold and windy in the mountains, they had lit fires and were lying down. Among the performers, one who suffered from the cold put on the costume of the Rākṣasa from their performance script and sat before the fire.

At that time, one among the traveling companions who had been asleep suddenly saw a rākṣasa by the side of the fire; failing to observe it closely, he abandoned it and fled, whereupon all his fellow travelers were startled and began to run away in every direction.

At that time, one among the companions who was wearing a rākṣasa’s garment also pursued them, running and galloping with great speed. Seeing him behind them, the fellow travelers thought he intended to harm them; their terror increased manifold as they leaped over mountains and rivers and threw themselves into ravines. Their bodies were wounded and torn, and they were utterly exhausted and prostrate until daybreak, when they finally realized it was not a ghost.

All ordinary beings are likewise: dwelling amidst the famine of afflictions that starve wholesome dharmas, they seek to find far away the food of the unsurpassed Dharma—permanence, bliss, self, and purity—and thus recklessly conceive a notion of "self" within the five aggregates.

Because of the view of self, one wanders through birth and death, pursued by afflictions and unable to attain mastery; one falls into the abysses of the three miserable realms and evil destinies. When the light of day appears—metaphorically signifying the exhaustion of the night of birth and death and the dawn of wisdom—one finally realizes that within the five aggregates there is no true self.

64. The Parable of the Old House with an Evil Spirit (64) The Parable of the Old House with an Evil Spirit: Once there was an old house, and people said that this chamber was always haunted by an evil spirit; everyone was terrified and dared not sleep there.
At that time, there was a man who considered himself bold and spoke these words:
"I wish to enter this room to lie down for one night.

He immediately entered and stayed there. Later, another man, considering his own courage superior to that of the former, heard from bystanders that an evil spirit constantly dwells within this room; he then desired to enter, pushed open the door, and stepped forward.
At that time, the one who had entered first thought it was a ghost and immediately pushed against the door to block him from proceeding;
the one who arrived later also thought there was a ghost, and the two men quarreled until daybreak.
Once they have seen one another, they finally realize that it was not a ghost.
All people of the world are likewise thus: meeting for a brief moment due to causes and conditions, there is no sovereign master; if one analyzes each part, who is "I"?
Nevertheless, sentient beings recklessly calculate right and wrong and forcibly give rise to disputes and litigation;

they are no different from those two people mentioned above. 65. The Parable of the Five Hundred Joy-pills (65). The Parable of the Five Hundred Joy-pills: Once there was a woman who was excessively licentious and unrestrained. Her lustful desires having become intense, she grew jealous and loathed her husband. She constantly contemplated schemes intending to harm him, yet despite devising various stratagems, she could find no opportunity.
She encountered her husband as he was being dispatched as an envoy to a neighboring state. The wife secretly devised a scheme to prepare poisonous pills, intending to harm her husband.

She spoke deceptively to him, saying: "As you are now on a distant mission, I fear you may lack sufficient provisions. I have prepared five hundred 'joy-pills' (ānanda-guḍa) to serve as travel rations for you; when you have left the country and reached the borders of another realm, you should eat them only when you are exhausted by hunger."

Following those words, they reached another realm; before they had even eaten it, they stopped overnight in a forest during the darkness of night. Fearing wild beasts, they climbed a tree to take refuge, but they forgot to place the *mṛṇāla-guḍikā* (joy-pills) beneath the tree.

That very night, five hundred bandits encountered them; having stolen five hundred horses and various treasures from the king of that country, they came to rest beneath the tree. Because they had fled in such haste, they were all exhausted by hunger and thirst. Seeing the *mṛdvīkā* (joy-pills) beneath the tree, the bandits took them and each ate one pill. The potency of the medicinal poison surged, and the five hundred bandits all died at once.

When dawn broke and the man atop the tree saw that the bandits were dead beneath it, he feigned having killed them with his sword and arrows; he then gathered their saddles, horses, and treasures, and drove them toward that country.
At that time, the king of that country led a great multitude of people along the tracks to pursue him. Meeting the king on the road, the king asked: "Who are you?"
"Where did you obtain this horse?
The man replied, "I am a native of such-and-such a country.

While traveling on the road, I encountered this band of thieves who were hacking and shooting at one another; these five hundred thieves now all lie dead together beneath a tree. For this reason, I have obtained this horse and these treasures and come to seek refuge in Your Majesty’s kingdom. If you do not yet believe me, you may send someone to inspect the place where the thieves’ wounds and the site of their slaughter are located."
The king immediately dispatched his trusted attendants to investigate, and it was indeed as he had said.

The king was delighted and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; once he returned to his kingdom, he generously bestowed upon him noble titles and rewards, granting him precious treasures and a village as a fief.
The king’s former ministers all became envious and said to the king:
“He is a man from afar and not yet worthy of trust; how can you suddenly show him such excessive favor, even to the point of surpassing the old ministers in rank and reward?”
Having heard this, the man from afar spoke these words:
"Who is there of brave and martial spirit who can test their strength with me?
I request that we compare our skills on a level plain."
The local men were struck with awe, and none dared to oppose him.

Later, in a vast wilderness within that kingdom, there was a ferocious lion that blocked the roads, killing people and cutting off the king’s highway. At that time, the former ministers deliberated together:
"That man from afar claims to be brave and strong, such that no one can match him; if he can now kill that lion and rid the kingdom of this harm, it would truly be extraordinary."
Having deliberated thus, they informed the king; upon hearing this, the king granted them weapons and immediately dispatched them.

At that time, having received the command, the man from afar resolved his mind with firm strength and set out for the lion’s location. Seeing him, the lion roared fiercely and lunged forward. The man was struck with terror and climbed a tree; the lion opened its mouth and raised its head toward the tree. In his panic, the man dropped the sword he was clutching, and it fell right into the lion’s mouth, whereupon the lion died instantly.

At that time, the people from afar were filled with joy and exultation; they came to inform the king, who treated them with redoubled favor, while the people of that land suddenly became respectful and submissive, all offering their praise.

The woman’s “joy-pills” are a metaphor for impure giving; the king’s dispatching of a messenger is a metaphor for a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); arriving in another country is a metaphor for [rebirth among] the various devas; slaying the bandits is a metaphor for attaining the stage of *srotāpanna*, forcefully severing the five desires along with all afflictions (*kleśa*); and encountering the king of that country is a metaphor for meeting with the worthy and the noble (*ārya*).

Those among the country’s long-established inhabitants who give rise to jealousy are likened to the various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who, upon seeing a person of wisdom capable of severing afflictions and the five desires, immediately give rise to slander, claiming that such a thing does not exist.

The "distant man" speaks with fierce resolve, saying that among the former ministers there is none capable of joining him as an adversary; this is a metaphor for how no heterodox teachers dare to confront or resist him.
The "slaying of the lion" is a metaphor for the destruction of Māra.
Having severed the afflictions and subdued the evil Māra, one obtains the reward of the fruit of the path of non-attachment.
One who is constantly fearful and timid is likened to one who is able to overcome the strong through weakness.

Although one may lack a pure mind at the outset, if that person’s giving encounters a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), they will obtain a superior reward; if even impure giving yields such results, how much more so when one gives with a virtuous mind and joyful devotion?
Therefore, one should diligently cultivate the practice of giving toward the field of merit.

This son of a householder is well-versed in the methods for entering the sea and handling ships; when entering waters where there are whirlpools, eddies, counter-currents, or turbulent rapids, he knows how to hold the helm, how to steer correctly, and how to maintain his position, saying to the multitude:

67. The Parable of the Husband and Wife Sharing Cakes (67) Once there was a husband and wife who had three cakes. They divided them together, each eating one cake, and one cake remained. They made a mutual agreement, saying:
"If either of us speaks, we shall not give the cake [to the other]."
Having made this agreement, neither dared to speak for the sake of a single cake.
In a short while, a thief entered the house and stole their wealth; everything they possessed fell entirely into the thief's hands.
Because of their prior agreement, the husband and wife watched with their own eyes but did not speak.
The thief saw him but did not speak; he then approached his wife and attempted to violate her. Although her husband saw this with his own eyes, he likewise remained silent.
The wife then called out to the thief and said to her husband, "How can you, a foolish man, fail to call out to the thief when you see him, all for the sake of a single cake?"
Her husband clapped his hands and laughed, saying, "Fie on you, slave!
I shall certainly have the cake; I will not give it to you anymore.
When the people of the world heard this, there was none who did not mock him.

Ordinary worldlings are just like this: for the sake of minor fame and profit, they falsely manifest stillness and silence; yet they are invaded by the various evil thieves of false afflictions, whereby they lose their wholesome dharmas and fall into the three miserable realms. They feel no fear at all and do not seek the path that transcends the world; instead, they remain attached to and dally in the five desires. Even when encountering great suffering, they do not regard it as a calamity, being no different from those foolish people mentioned before.
68. The Parable of Mutual Enmity and Harm (68) The Parable of Mutual Enmity and Harm: Once upon a time, there was a man who became angry with another; he was filled with grief and found no joy.
Someone asked him,
"For what reason are you now so dejected and haggard?
He replied to them immediately:
"A person has disparaged me, yet my power is insufficient to retaliate; I do not know by what means I might take revenge, and for this reason I am sorrowful.
Another person said to him:
"Only the Vidyā-mantra can harm him, but there is one drawback: before it can harm him, it will instead turn back and harm you yourself."
Upon hearing this, the man was filled with great joy and said, "I only wish that you would teach me; even if it means harming myself, I desire to wound him.

People of the world are just like this: for the sake of anger, they seek the Vidyādhara spells in order to torment others; yet before they have ever harmed another, they first harm themselves through their own wrath, falling into the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts—no different from that foolish man.

69. The Parable of Eating Rapidly to Imitate One’s Ancestors (69) The Parable of Eating Rapidly to Imitate One’s Ancestors: Once upon a time, there was a man who traveled from North India to South India. Having resided there for a long time, he married a local woman and lived as her husband.
At that time, the wife prepared food and drink for her husband; the husband, upon receiving it, swallowed it hurriedly without avoiding its heat.
The wife, finding this strange, said to her husband:
"There are no thieves here to plunder you; what urgent matter is there that you are so rushed and do not eat calmly and leisurely?"
The husband replied to his wife, "I have a secret matter that I cannot tell you.
When the wife heard these words, she thought there must be some extraordinary matter; she questioned him earnestly, and only after a long while did he answer:
"My grandfather and his predecessors have always eaten quickly; I am now following their example, and that is why I am fast.

Worldly ordinary people are just like this: failing to comprehend correct principles and ignorant of good and evil, they commit various perverse acts without shame, claiming, "My grandfather and his predecessors practiced such a way; I shall follow it until death and never abandon it," just as that foolish man practiced eating quickly, taking it to be a virtuous custom.
70. The Parable of Tasting the Āmra Fruit Once there was an elder who sent a man with money to another’s garden to buy an *āmra* fruit so that he might eat it. He gave him this instruction:
“You must buy one that is sweet and delicious.”
He then took the money and went to buy some of the fruit.
The owner of the orchard said, "All the fruit on this tree is excellent; there is not a single bad one. You need only taste one fruit to know this for yourself."
The fruit-buyer said, "I must now taste each one individually before I take them; how could I know otherwise by tasting only one?
He then immediately took the fruits and tasted each one, carrying them back home.
When the elder saw this, he loathed it and would not eat it, subsequently discarding it all.

People of the world are just like this: hearing that by observing the precepts and practicing generosity one attains great wealth and happiness, and that one’s person remains constantly secure and free from all afflictions, they are unwilling to believe it, saying instead:
"If giving brings merit, I shall only believe it when I have attained it myself."

"Beholding with one's own eyes that the nobility, the lowly, the wealthy, and the poor in this present life are all the retributive fruits obtained from past karma, yet they do not know to trace back to seek the cause and effect; thus they harbor disbelief until they must experience it for themselves. Once their lives end, their wealth and possessions are lost, just as one who has tasted the fruit must abandon it all."

71. The Parable of Losing Both Eyes for the Sake of Two Wives (71) The Parable of Losing Both Eyes for the Sake of Two Wives: Once there was a man who took two wives. If he drew near to one, he would be resented by the other.
Unable to decide between them, he lay down with his body upright in the middle of the two women.

It happened that it was raining heavily, and the roof leaked; as both water and mud fell into his eyes, he did not dare rise to avoid them because of his prior vow, and consequently lost the sight of both his eyes.

Ordinary worldlings are just like this: by associating with evil friends and practicing what is not the Dharma, they create karmic fetters and fall into the three evil realms; dwelling long in birth and death, they lose the eye of wisdom, just as that foolish man lost both eyes for the sake of his two wives.
72. Oṃ mi khyod ku yu (72). Oṃ mi khyod ku yu. Once upon a time, there was a man who went to his wife’s family home; seeing them pounding rice, he went to that place and stole some rice to eat.

When his wife came to see him and wished to converse with him, his mouth was full of rice and he could not respond at all; out of shame before his wife, he was unwilling to spit it out, and for this reason he remained silent.
The wife, wondering why he did not speak, felt his mouth with her hand and thought it was swollen;
she said to her father, "My husband, as soon as he arrived, suddenly developed a swelling in his mouth and can no longer speak at all."
The father immediately summoned a physician to treat him.
The physician said, "This illness is most grave; it can only be cured by cutting it open with a knife."
He then used a knife to slit open the man's mouth, and as the rice came out from within, the matter was exposed.

People of the world are just like this: having committed various evil deeds and violated the pure precepts, they conceal their transgressions and refuse to reveal them, thereby falling into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
Just as that fool, out of a slight sense of shame, refused to spit out the rice, he had to have his mouth slit open with a knife before his transgression was revealed.

73. The Parable of Falsely Claiming a Horse’s Death (73) Once there was a man who rode a black horse into battle to strike at the enemy. Because of his fear, he was unable to fight; he then smeared blood upon his face and body to falsely manifest the appearance of death, lying among the corpses. The horse he was riding was seized by others.
Once the army had departed and he was about to return home, he immediately cut off the tail of another man’s white horse and brought it with him.
Upon arriving at his house, someone asked him, "Where is the horse you were riding? Why are you not riding it?"
He replied,
"My horse has died, so I have brought its tail.
A bystander said to him:
“Your horse was originally black; why is its tail white?
He remained silent and offered no reply, becoming an object of ridicule for others.

People of the world are just like this: they claim to be practicing the cultivation of a compassionate mind and abstaining from wine and meat, yet they slaughter sentient beings and inflict upon them bitter suffering. They falsely call themselves virtuous while committing every kind of evil, just like that fool who deceitfully claimed his horse had died.

74. The Parable of the Householder Layman Craving Gain (Seventy-four) Once there was a king who established a legal code: all brahmins and others within his realm were strictly prohibited from bathing; those who did not bathe were driven away and compelled to perform various forms of forced labor.
There was a brahmin who, while empty-handedly clutching a ritual water vessel, falsely claimed he had washed it clean. When people poured water into it for him, he immediately spat it out and said:
"I did not wash it clean; the King shall wash it himself!"
For the sake of the king’s favor and to avoid royal service, they falsely claim to have been purified when in truth they have not.

So it is with the ordinary worldling who has left the household life: though he has shaved his head and donned the dyed robes, within he actually violates the prohibitions. Deceitfully manifesting the observance of precepts, he hopes for gain and offerings; furthermore, like one avoiding royal service, he appears outwardly to be a śramaṇa while being inwardly hollow and fraudulent—like grasping an empty bottle that possesses only external form.

75. The Parable of the Camel and the Jar (Seventy-Five) The Parable of the Camel and the Jar: Once upon a time, there was a man who had previously filled a jar with grain. A camel thrust its head into the jar to eat the grain, but it could not get its head out. Unable to extricate itself, the camel became distressed and troubled by its predicament.
An old man came and said to him:
"Do not grieve! I shall teach you how to escape;
if you follow my words, you will surely emerge quickly. You must cut off your own head, and thus you will get out."
He then followed those words, using a knife to cut off his own head, further killing the camel and breaking the jar.
Such a fool is laughed at by the world. Ordinary, ignorant people are just like this:

they aspire to Bodhi and seek the Three Vehicles with earnest intent, and ought to maintain the prohibitive precepts to guard against all evils; yet, for the sake of the five desires, they violate their pure precepts. Having transgressed the prohibitions, they abandon the Three Vehicles and give rein to their hearts and minds, committing every kind of evil. Thus, both the vehicle and the pure precepts are discarded, just as that foolish man lost both the camel and the jar.

76. The Parable of the Farmer Who Longed for the King’s Daughter Once, there was a farmer who traveled through cities and towns. There he beheld the king’s daughter, whose countenance was so upright and beautiful that she was a rarity in the world. Day and night his thoughts were fixed upon her, and his longing could not be stilled. He longed to have union with her, but finding no means to achieve it, his complexion turned sallow and yellow, and he fell gravely ill.
Those who witnessed this personally asked the man,
"Why is it like this?
He replied to his relatives:
"Yesterday I saw the king's daughter; her countenance was upright and beautiful. Because I desired to have union with her but could not obtain it, I am thus ill.
If I do not obtain her, my death is certain beyond doubt."
The relatives said, "We shall devise a skillful means for you so that you may obtain it; do not be distressed.
Later, when they saw him, they spoke to him, saying:
"We have already achieved our purpose for your sake; it is only that the princess does not desire you.
Upon hearing this, the farmer smiled with joy, saying to himself, "I shall surely obtain her."

The foolish people of the world are just like this: failing to distinguish between the seasons of spring, autumn, winter, and summer, they cast seeds into the earth during the winter in hopes of obtaining fruit. In vain they waste their labor and achieve nothing; they lose everything—the sprouts, stems, branches, and leaves alike.

Foolish people of the world, practicing only a small amount of merit, consider themselves complete; they then claim that awakening can already be realized, like that farmer who longed for the king’s daughter.

77. The Parable of Milking a Donkey (77). The Parable of Milking a Donkey: Once, there was a person from a remote borderland who did not know what a donkey was. Hearing others say that donkey’s milk was exceedingly delicious, he knew nothing of it at all.

At that time, the people obtained a single old donkey and wished to milk it; they struggled together to seize it, some grasping its head, some its ears, some its tail, and some its legs, while others grasped the vessel, each desiring to be the first to drink from it.
In the midst of this, he seized the donkey’s penis, thinking it was a teat, and immediately began to milk it in his hope of obtaining milk.
The multitude grew weary and exhausted, yet they obtained nothing at all; they merely labored in vain without any gain, becoming an object of ridicule for all the people of the world.

The non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings are just like this: hearing it said that one should not seek the Way in such places, they give rise to false conceptions and various wrong views—such as going naked, starving themselves, throwing themselves from cliffs, or leaping into fire—and because of these wrong views, they fall into the evil realms, just like those foolish people who falsely sought milk.

78. The Parable of the Man Who Agreed with His Son to Travel Early (78) The Parable of the Man Who Agreed with His Son to Travel Early: Once upon a time, there was a man who spoke to his son at night, saying:
"Tomorrow, I shall go with you to that village to fetch something."
Having heard these words, at dawn the next morning, the son went alone to that place without asking his father.

Upon arriving there, his body was utterly exhausted and he returned empty-handed; furthermore, having failed to obtain food, he was so hungry and thirsty that he was on the verge of death when he finally turned back to see his father.
Seeing his son approaching, the father rebuked him deeply, saying:
"You are utterly foolish and devoid of wisdom; why did you not wait for me?
You have come and gone in vain, suffering in vain, and become an object of ridicule for all people in the world."

Ordinary worldlings are also like this: even if they manage to leave the household life by shaving their hair and beards and donning the three dharma robes, they do not seek out an enlightened teacher to inquire about and receive the teachings of the Way. Consequently, they lose all the merits of the meditative concentrations and the factors of enlightenment; they lose all the sublime fruits of a śramaṇa. Like that foolish man who makes a vain journey and merely exhausts himself in toil, they appear to be śramaṇas in form, yet in reality have attained nothing.

79. The Parable of the King Carrying a Stool (79) The Parable of the King Carrying a Stool: Once there was a king who, wishing to enter an *aśoka* grove to enjoy himself in pleasure, commanded a minister, saying:
"Take a stool and carry it to that grove; I shall sit and rest there."
At that time, the messenger felt ashamed and was unwilling to grasp it, so he said to the king, "I cannot grasp it;
I wish instead to carry it on my back.
Thereupon, the king placed thirty-six stools upon his back and compelled him to carry them to the garden.

In this way, such a fool is ridiculed by the world; ordinary people are just like this. If they see a single strand of a woman’s hair on the ground, they claim to observe the precepts and refuse to touch it;

yet later, deluded by afflictions, they do not consider the thirty-six impure substances—hair, fur, nails, teeth, excrement, and urine—to be loathsome. They grasp all thirty-six substances at once without feeling shame or remorse, clinging to them until death, just like that fool who carried the table upon his shoulders.
80. The Parable of the Retrograde Enema (80). Once there was a man suffering from a disease of the lower parts.
A physician said to him, "You must undergo a retrograde enema before you can be cured."
He then gathered the medicinal decoction, intending to administer it;
however, before the physician had even arrived, he took it by himself. His belly swelled until he was on the verge of death, unable to endure the pain.
When the physician finally arrived, marvelling at the cause of his condition, he immediately questioned him:
"Why is this so? he asked. The physician replied:
"Just now, when the medicine was poured out, I took it and swallowed it; that is why I wish to die."
When the physician heard these words, he rebuked him deeply, saying:
"You are a great fool who does not understand skillful means.
He then administered other medicines, and only after the patient had vomited and purged did he finally recover.

Such a foolish person is laughed at by the world; ordinary people are likewise so. When they wish to practice various methods of meditative contemplation (*dhyāna-vipaśyanā*), they should emulate the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) but instead emulate breath-counting (*ānāpānasmṛti*); those who should be counting the breath instead emulate the contemplation of the six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*). Thus, with their practice inverted from top to bottom and lacking any foundation, they merely waste their lives, becoming entangled and distressed by such errors.
To practice inverted methods of meditation without consulting a virtuous teacher is like that foolish man who drank and consumed filth.

81. The Parable of Being Bitten by a Bear (81): The Parable of Being Bitten by a Bear. Once, there were a father and son traveling together with companions. The son entered a forest and was bitten by a bear; his body was mangled by its claws. In great distress, he emerged from the forest and returned to his companions.
When the father saw that his son’s body was mangled and wounded, he asked him in astonishment,
"For what reason have you now been afflicted by these sores?
The son replied to his father:
"There is a creature with long, shaggy body hair that comes to harm me.
The father took his bow and arrows and went into the forest; there he saw a seer whose hair was deep and long, and he immediately intended to shoot him.
A bystander said, "Why do you shoot him? This man is harmless;
you should instead punish those who have committed an offense."

The foolish people of the world are likewise: though they revile those who wear the dharma-robes but lack the practice of the Way, they indiscriminately harm virtuous and worthy persons; this is like that father bear who injured his own child and unjustly brought calamity upon the divine seer.
82. Parable of the Farmer (82): The Parable of the Farmer In the past, there was a rustic man who came to a field and saw that the wheat seedlings were growing lush and flourishing.
He asked the owner of the wheat, "How do you manage to make this wheat so lush and fine?"
The owner replied, "I leveled the ground and applied manure and water; that is why it has become like this.

The man then proceeded to use the method according to the instructions: he moistened the field with water and manure and sowed the seeds in the earth. Fearing that treading on the ground with his own feet would make the soil too hard for the wheat to grow, he thought, "I shall sit upon a couch and have it carried by porters; from there I will scatter the seeds, and only then will it be well."

Even when four men each lifted one leg and went to the field to scatter the seeds, the ground became even harder, leading others to mock them, fearing that their own two feet had been increased by eight.

Ordinary worldlings are just like this: once they have cultivated the field of precepts and the sprouts of goodness are about to emerge, they ought to consult their teachers and receive their instructions so that the sprouts of the Dharma may grow;

yet instead, they violate them and commit many evils, thereby preventing the sprouts of the precepts from arising—just as that man feared his two feet being overturned and instead added eight more upon them.
83. The Parable of the Monkey (83). Once there was a monkey who, having been beaten by an adult, could do nothing about it; instead, he resented a small child.

Ordinary, foolish people are just like this: the person they previously hated has passed away and ceased without ceasing, yet they continue to perceive the subsequent states in that continuum as being that same former person, and thus give rise to false anger and resentment, their poisonous hatred becoming ever deeper—just like that foolish monkey who, having been struck by a large man, instead turned its wrath upon a small child.
84. The Parable of the Lunar Eclipse and the Beating of a Dog In the past, when the Asura King saw the sun and moon shining with pure brilliance, he sought to obstruct them with his hands.
Likewise, ignorant commoners inflict evil upon others despite their innocence, like a dog being beaten for no fault of its own.

Ordinary worldlings are likewise: driven by greed, hatred, and delusion, they afflict their bodies with suffering, lying upon thorns and pricking them with fivefold heat, just like that dog who was unjustly beaten during the lunar eclipse.
85. The Parable of the Woman Suffering from Eye Pain Once there was a woman who suffered greatly from eye pain. A female acquaintance asked her, “Are your eyes painful?”
He replied, "My eyes ache. She spoke again:
"One who has eyes will inevitably suffer pain; although I do not yet feel it, I wish to pluck out my eyes for fear of future suffering.
A bystander said to him:
"If the eyes remain, one may or may not experience pain; but if the eyes are gone, one will suffer eternal pain."

Ordinary, foolish people are just like this: hearing that wealth and nobility are the root of decline and suffering, they fear not practicing generosity lest they receive retribution later, and thus, despite their overflowing riches, they undergo intense suffering.
Someone might say to you:
"If you practice giving, there may be suffering or pleasure; if you do not give, there will be the great suffering of poverty.
Just as that woman, unable to endure the immediate pain, wished to remove her eyes, only to bring about long-term suffering.

86. The Parable of the Father Taking the Son’s Earring (86) Once, there were two people, a father and a son, traveling together on business. Suddenly, bandits rose up on the road, intending to plunder them. The son wore a genuine gold earring in his ear; seeing the bandits suddenly appear, the father feared he would lose the earring and immediately pulled at it with his hand. Because the earring did not come out immediately, the father cut off the son’s head for the sake of that earring. In a mere moment, the bandits abandoned their pursuit and departed. The father then placed the son’s head upon his shoulder, but it could not be restored.
In this way, such fools are ridiculed by the world. Ordinary persons are likewise;

for the sake of fame and profit, they engage in frivolous discourse, claiming that the two worlds exist or do not exist, that the intermediate state exists or does not exist, and that mental factors exist or do not exist. Through various such delusions, they fail to attain the reality of dharmas.
When others refute his argument with a discourse in accordance with the Dharma, he says:
"In my treatise, there was never such a statement.

Thus, for the sake of minor fame and profit, this fool deliberately utters falsehoods, thereby destroying the fruits of the śramaṇa path; at the dissolution of the body after death, he falls into the three evil realms, just as that fool, for the sake of a small gain, severed the head of his own son.

87. The Parable of the Robbers Dividing Their Loot Once, there was a band of robbers who went together to commit a robbery. Having taken a great deal of wealth, they divided it equally among themselves. There was only one *kambala* cloth from Rājagṛha that was not of pure or fine quality; this they set aside as the inferior portion and gave it to the lowest-ranking member.
The inferior one, upon obtaining it, felt resentment and regret, crying out that he had suffered a great loss; he went to the city to sell it.
There, many noble elders offered him a high price, so that what he received was twice as much as all his companions combined. Only then did he rejoice with immeasurable joy and exultation.

It is just as when people in the world, not knowing whether giving alms yields a reward or not, practice only a small act of charity and thereby attain birth in the heavens to experience immeasurable bliss; only then do they feel regret, lamenting that they did not give more extensively.
Just as one feels great joy upon obtaining a high price for a piece of *kambala* wool cloth;
so too it is with giving: when one gives little and receives much in return, one then rejoices within oneself, regretting only that one did not give more.

88. The Parable of the Monkey Holding Beans (88) The Parable of the Monkey Holding Beans: Once there was a monkey who held a handful of beans. By mistake, he let one bean fall to the ground; immediately, he cast aside the beans in his hand, intending to search for that single one. Before he could find it, the previously discarded bean had been eaten up by chickens and ducks.

The renunciation of an ordinary person is just like this: having initially violated a single precept, they are unable to repent. Because they do not repent, their negligence spreads and overruns until they abandon everything, just as that monkey, having lost one bean, abandoned them all.

89. The Parable of Finding a Golden Weasel (89) The Parable of Finding a Golden Weasel: Once upon a time, there was a man traveling along a road who found a golden weasel in his path. His heart leaped with joy, and he took it up, placing it within his bosom. Continuing on his way, he reached a body of water he wished to cross; he removed his clothes and set them upon the ground. At that very moment, the golden weasel transformed into a venomous serpent.
This person reflected deeply:
"I would rather be killed by a venomous snake than depart with this [object] in my arms.
His mind was moved by a profound and mysterious resonance, and it transformed back into gold.

A foolish person standing nearby, seeing that the poisonous snake had been transformed into a genuine jewel, thought it would always remain so; he then took the poisonous snake and placed it within his bosom, whereupon he was bitten by the snake and lost his life.

The foolish people of the world are likewise: seeing that doing good brings profit, they lack sincerity within; they merely associate with the Dharma for the sake of gain and sustenance, and after their lives end, they fall into evil realms, like one who seizes a poisonous snake and dies from its sting.

90. The Parable of Finding Money on the Road Once, there was a poor man traveling along a road who happened to find a bag of gold coins. Overjoyed, he immediately began counting them; before he had finished, the owner of the money suddenly arrived and seized it all back from him. At that moment, the man regretted not having fled more quickly, and his feelings of anguish were most extreme.

It is the same for those who encounter the Buddha-dharma: although they have met with the Triple Gem, the field of merit, if they do not diligently apply skillful means to practice wholesome deeds, they will suddenly meet their end and fall into the three evil realms—just like that foolish man whose master took back his money and departed.
As it is said in the verse:
"Today one attends to this matter; tomorrow one undertakes that.
Delighting in attachment and failing to contemplate suffering, one does not perceive the arrival of the thief of death."
Hastily attending to various affairs—there is no ordinary person who does not do so.
Just like that man counting his coins, such is the nature of their business. 91.

The Parable of the Poor Man Who Wishes to Equal the Wealth of the Rich (91) The Parable of the Poor Man Who Wishes to Equal the Wealth of the Rich: Once there was a poor man who possessed only a small amount of wealth. Seeing a great wealthy man, he desired to be equal to him; yet because he could not achieve equality, he wished to cast even his meager possessions into the water.
A bystander said, "Although this object is meager, it could prolong your life for several days; why do you discard it and throw it into the water?

The foolish people of the world are just like this: although they have left the household life and obtained a small measure of offerings, their minds harbor expectations and are constantly filled with a sense of insufficiency; they are unable to equal those of high virtue in obtaining such offerings.

Seeing others who are long-established and virtuous, possessing extensive learning and receiving abundant offerings from the masses, one feels a desire to equal them; yet, being unable to do so, the mind harbors sorrow and suffering, leading one to wish to abandon the path—just as that foolish man, wishing to equal a wealthy person, casts away his own wealth.

92. The Parable of the Child Receiving a Delightful Ball (92) The Parable of the Child Receiving a Delightful Ball: Once upon a time, a wet nurse was carrying a child along a road. Becoming utterly exhausted from the journey, she fell fast asleep without realizing it.

At that time, there was a man who gave a *modaka* (joy-pill) to a young child; having received it, the child, craving its delicious flavor, paid no heed to his own body or possessions, whereupon the man immediately removed his shackles and chains and took away all his necklaces and garments.

It is the same with the bhikṣu: if he delights in places of bustle and busy affairs, and covets small gains and offerings, the thieves of affliction will seize his precious necklaces of merit and precepts, just as those children, because they coveted a little taste, had all their possessions carried away by the thieves.

93. The Parable of the Old Woman Catching the Bear Once upon a time, there was an old woman sleeping beneath a tree when a bear came to seize her. At that moment, the old woman ran around the tree to escape; the bear followed closely behind, reaching out one paw to grasp her as it tried to catch her. In her desperation, the old woman immediately pressed both of the bear’s paws against the trunk of the tree, so that the bear could not move.
Furthermore, another person came to that place, and the old woman said to him, "Help me seize him;
we shall kill him and divide his flesh.
At that time, the man believed the old woman's words and immediately joined her in seizing him.
Once he had caught it, the old woman immediately abandoned the bear and fled, while the man was subsequently trapped by the bear.
Thus, such a foolish person is ridiculed by the world.

Ordinary people are just like this: they compose various heterodox treatises that are neither skillful nor refined; their prose is cumbersome and riddled with many flaws, such that before the work is even finished, they pass away and abandon it. When later generations take up these works intending to explain them, they fail to grasp the intended meaning and instead become entangled in difficulties—just like that foolish man who took another's bear by the paw and was himself harmed by it.

94. The Parable of the Maṇi Water Drain (94) The Parable of the Maṇi Water Drain: Once there was a man who had an illicit affair with another’s wife. Before their union was complete, her husband returned from outside. He immediately became aware of them and stood outside the door, waiting for the moment she emerged so that he might kill her.
The wife said to the man:
"My husband has already woken up; there is no other way out. Only the *maṇi* can be used to escape—the *maṇi* being what everyone calls the opening of the water conduit."

He wished for that person to emerge through the drain, but the person misunderstood, thinking it was a *maṇi* jewel; he searched everywhere for it but could not find its location, and immediately said:
"I will never leave until I see the *maṇi* jewel."
"In a mere moment, he was killed by it.
Ordinary people are just like this: someone might say to them, 'Within birth and death there is impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self;
one should avoid the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism and abide in the Middle Way; by passing through this middle way, one may attain liberation.'"

Ordinary people misunderstand this and seek whether the world is finite or infinite, and whether sentient beings possess a self or are selfless; they ultimately fail to contemplate the principle of the Middle Way. Suddenly meeting their end, they are slain by impermanence and fall into the three evil realms, just like that foolish man who sought the *maṇi* jewel and was consequently harmed by others.

95. The Parable of the Two Pigeons (95) The Parable of the Two Pigeons: Once upon a time, there were a male and a female pigeon sharing a single nest. When the autumn fruits ripened, they gathered fruit until the nest was full. Later, when the fruit had dried and diminished, only half remained in the nest. The male became angry and said to the female:
"You have worked hard gathering this fruit, yet you have eaten it all alone; only half remains."
The female pigeon replied, "I do not eat alone; the fruit has indeed diminished.
The male pigeon did not believe her and spoke with anger:
"It is not that you alone eat [the pigeons]; by what means could they have diminished?
He then pecked at a female pigeon with his beak and killed her.
Before many days had passed, a great rain fell from the heavens; indeed, they became moistened and returned to their former state. Upon seeing this, the male pigeon finally gave rise to regret.
"He did not actually eat it; I have falsely killed another.
Thus he cried out in grief, calling to his female dove: "Where have you gone? Ordinary people are just like this:

harboring delusions in their hearts, they falsely grasp at sensual pleasures without contemplating impermanence. Having violated the grave prohibitions, what can be achieved by repenting later? What use is it?
Later, he could only lament like that foolish pigeon. 96.

The Parable of Falsely Pretending to Be Blind (96). Once there was a master craftsman who, unable to endure the hardships of his service for the king, falsely claimed to be blind and thereby escaped his suffering.
Another master, hearing of this, wished to gouge out his own eyes to avoid forced labor.
Someone said to him:
"Why do you destroy yourself?"
They merely undergo suffering.
Thus the foolish person is ridiculed by the world. Ordinary people are just like this:

for the sake of a little reputation and material gain, they deliberately speak falsehoods and destroy their pure precepts; when their bodies die and their lives end, they fall into the three evil realms, just as that fool destroyed his own eyes for the sake of a small profit.

97. The Parable of Losing a Woolen Cloth to Bandits (97) The Parable of Losing a Woolen Cloth to Bandits: Once, there were two men traveling together as companions through a vast wilderness. One man was wearing a single woolen cloth (*karpāsa*), but midway through their journey, he was stripped of it by bandits. The other man fled and hid himself within the grass.
The one who had lost the cotton cloth had previously wrapped a single gold coin inside the hem of the garment;
he then said to the thief, "This robe is worth exactly one gold coin; I now seek to redeem it for that one gold coin."
The bandits asked,
"Where is the gold coin now?
He immediately untied it from his turban, showed it to them, and said to the bandits:
"This is genuine gold; if you do not believe my words, there is a skilled goldsmith here among the grasses whom you may go to ask.
Once the thief saw him, he took his robe back as well.
In this way, the foolish man loses both the cotton cloth and the gold coins; he not only loses his own profit but causes the other to lose theirs as well. Ordinary worldlings are just like this:

though they practice the factors of enlightenment and cultivate various merits, they are plundered by the thieves of affliction. They lose their wholesome dharmas and forfeit all their merits; not only do they lose their own benefit, but they also cause others to lose their spiritual path. When their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the three evil realms, just as that foolish man lost everything for both himself and the other.

98. The Parable of the Boy Who Caught a Large Turtle (98) Once upon a time, there was a young boy who, while playing on dry land, caught a large turtle. Desiring to kill it, he did not know the proper means and asked someone, "How can I kill it?"
Someone said to him, "If you simply throw it into the water, you can kill it immediately.
At that time, because the boy believed those words, he threw it into the water; once the tortoise reached the water, it immediately swam away.

Ordinary people are just like this: desiring to guard the six sense faculties and cultivate various merits, yet lacking understanding of skillful means, they ask others, "By what causes and conditions can one attain liberation?"
Heterodox practitioners with wrong views, the celestial Mara Pāpīyān, and evil associates spoke to him, saying:
"You need only indulge your mind in the six sense objects and gratify your desires for the five sensual pleasures; if you act according to my words, you will surely attain liberation."

Thus, these foolish people, failing to reflect with discernment, act upon those words; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the three evil realms, just like that child who threw the turtle into the water.
This treatise was composed by me; blending it with words of laughter and jest diminishes the true and correct teaching.
One should examine whether the meaning is appropriate or not, just as when bitter poison is mixed with rock honey.
Medicine is for the destruction of disease; this treatise is likewise.
To jest within the True Dharma is like that delirious drug;
the Buddha’s True Dharma is tranquil and stable, illuminating the world.
Just as when one has taken emetic or purgative medicine, ghee is used to moisten the interior of the body,
so now, by means of this principle, I shall manifest and clarify tranquil concentration.
It is like an agada medicine wrapped within tree leaves.
Having taken the medicine and applied the antidote, one discards the tree leaves.
Like the wrapping of leaves used in jest, the true meaning lies within;
the wise take the correct principle and should discard the jest.
The Venerable Saṃghasena has completed the composition of the *Mūḍhamañjarī* (The Garland of Fools).
The *Śatopamāsūtra* (Sutra of One Hundred Parables), Volume Four.
